title: Pick Shopify for a hosted, fast launch with no WordPress ties
hypothesis: If we choose Shopify when the brand has no WordPress site to keep and no in house dev team, then time to a working checkout drops because payments, tax service, and checkout ship built in.
does_not_apply_when: Brand already runs a WordPress site it must keep
Brand needs full control over every page element

signal.check: No platform is chosen yet, and the brand has no existing WordPress site or in house developer.

risk.note: Switching platforms later means a costly rebuild, so this decision should not be revisited casually.

prerequisites: Brand's existing site status confirmed
Checkout customization needs known
steps: Check if the brand already runs a WordPress site it must keep.
Check if custom checkout control beyond Shopify's default is a hard requirement.
Check if the brand has staff to maintain hosting, plugins, and security.
If none of these block Shopify, pick Shopify as the default.
Record the decision and the trade offs accepted in the store build brief.

test.method: Compare time from account signup to a completed test order against the WooCommerce path for a similar brand.
test.measure: days from signup to first real order

title: Pick WooCommerce when the brand needs full design control
hypothesis: If we choose WooCommerce when a page builder and plugin choice matter more than a managed stack, then the brand gets the control it needs because it owns hosting and every plugin.
does_not_apply_when: Brand has no staff or budget to maintain hosting, plugins, SMTP, backups, and security

signal.check: The brand wants full page and plugin control, already owns hosting, or must stay on WordPress.

risk.note: No WooCommerce source covers security, backups, or speed beyond basic hygiene, so ongoing upkeep falls on the brand.

prerequisites: Hosting account owned by the brand
Someone able to maintain plugins and SMTP
steps: Confirm the brand owns or will own its hosting account.
Confirm someone can maintain plugin updates, SMTP, backups, and security.
Pick the page builder (Elementor or the block editor) once, since it locks the editor for later pages.
Record the decision and the trade offs accepted in the store build brief.

test.method: Track the hours spent on plugin, SMTP, and security fixes in the first month.

title: Compare total cost of ownership, not just hosting price
hypothesis: If we price the full stack for 12 months on each platform, then the platform choice moves margin because plan fees, card rates, apps, hosting, plugins, and developer time all add up differently.

signal.check: A platform decision is being made using only a headline hosting or plan price, with no full cost comparison done.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no source gives this comparison

risk.note: This is a comparison exercise, not a platform change.

prerequisites: Current plan, app, and hosting prices checked live
steps: List Shopify plan fee, card rate at expected volume, and the 3 launch app prices for 12 months.
List hosting, paid plugins (table rate shipping, tax service, swatches, SMTP, security), and developer hours for 12 months.
Web check every price, since hosting and plan promos are dated and tied to affiliate terms.
Compare the two totals before committing to a platform.

test.method: Recheck the same comparison at 6 and 12 months against actual spend.

title: Pick a theme and platform the brand can keep for years
hypothesis: If we shortlist themes against the catalog size expected 4 to 5 years out, then rework and migration cost drops later because the theme will not need replacing as the catalog grows.

signal.check: A theme or platform is being chosen with no thought to catalog growth 4 to 5 years out.

risk.note: This only shapes the shortlist; it does not lock in a theme.

prerequisites: Rough catalog size target for the next few years
steps: Estimate catalog size and complexity 4 to 5 years out, not just at launch.
Shortlist themes and platforms that can support that size without a rebuild.
Note the trade off accepted if a cheaper, smaller-scale option is chosen instead.

test.method: Revisit the theme fit whenever catalog size doubles.

title: Migrate catalogue, orders, and SEO redirects before replatforming
hypothesis: If we migrate the product catalogue, order history, customer accounts, and SEO redirects to the new store before pointing the domain at it, then organic traffic and order history survive the switch because search engines and returning customers do not hit dead links or lost accounts.
does_not_apply_when: This is a brand's first ever store launch, not a replacement of an existing site

signal.check: A brand is replacing an existing website or platform rather than launching for the first time.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no library source, verify against brand data

risk.note: Missing redirects or lost order history after the domain switch cannot be recovered once search engines re-crawl.

prerequisites: Full export of the old store's catalogue, orders, and customer accounts
List of the old store's URLs to redirect
steps: Export the product catalogue, order history, and customer accounts from the old store.
Import them into the new store and verify counts match.
Build a 301 redirect map from every old URL to its new equivalent.
Test the redirects before pointing the domain at the new store.
Point the domain at the new store only after the above checks pass.

test.method: Track organic sessions and 404 errors for 8 weeks after the switch.
test.read_point: 4 and 8 weeks after the domain switch

title: Sign up with an email the business will always control
hypothesis: If we sign up with an email the business will still hold in years, not a contractor's or agency's, then critical account actions stay safe because only the owner can change currency, delete the store, or take other critical actions.

signal.check: The account being set up, or an inherited account, is tied to a contractor's or agency's email rather than the business owner's.

risk.note: Ownership transfer is possible later but takes extra steps and can be blocked if the wrong party controls the email.

steps: Pick an email address the business will still control after any contractor or agency is gone.
Use that email to sign up.
If the account already exists under a contractor's email, start an ownership transfer now, not at launch.

test.method: Check the account owner email against the business's own domain.

title: Enter exact legal identity before touching payments or tax
hypothesis: If we enter the exact legal business name and registered address before configuring payments, tax, or shipping, then payment verification goes faster because those screens use the identity fields as their default.

signal.check: Payments, tax, or shipping setup is starting before the legal name and address are entered in store settings.

risk.note: Fields can be edited later, but payments verification may need to restart.

prerequisites: Legal business name, registered address, and business number on hand
steps: Get the exact legal business name and registered address from the brand record.
Enter them in store settings before opening payments, tax, or shipping setup.
Confirm the entries match government or registration documents exactly.

test.method: Check that payments verification does not bounce for a name or address mismatch.
test.read_point: After the first payments verification attempt

title: Choose the store's permanent handle with care
hypothesis: If we choose the myshopify handle carefully at signup, then later confusion drops because the handle is permanent and support and apps reference it even after the customer facing name changes.

signal.check: A Shopify signup is in progress and the handle has not been chosen deliberately yet.

risk.note: The handle cannot be changed after signup, only the customer facing store name can.

steps: Draft 2 or 3 handle options based on the brand name before signup.
Pick the clearest, most permanent-feeling option.
Use it at signup, knowing the customer facing name can still change later.

test.method: Check the handle is never referenced by name in customer facing material.

title: Start on the cheapest plan, upgrade only on a real trigger
hypothesis: If we start a store with no revenue on the cheapest plan, then fixed cost drops because upgrades only pay off once staff seats, card rate, or plan-gated features actually justify the higher tier.

signal.check: A new store with no revenue is being set up on a mid or top plan tier by default.

expected_effect.size: unknown, plan prices need a web check

risk.note: Plans can be upgraded or downgraded later.

prerequisites: Current plan prices and feature gates checked live
steps: Start on the entry plan for a store with no revenue yet.
Track staff seat count, order volume, and any plan-gated feature the brand actually needs.
Upgrade only when one of those triggers is hit, not on a schedule.

test.method: Track plan cost against revenue each month for the first 6 months.

title: Audit an inherited account's real features before relying on the plan name
hypothesis: If we audit the actual feature set in settings for an inherited or migrated account, then setup mistakes drop because legacy accounts can carry inconsistent entitlements that do not match the plan name.
does_not_apply_when: This is a brand new account with no inherited or migrated history

signal.check: The account being worked on is old, migrated, or inherited from a previous owner or agency.

risk.note: An audit does not change anything by itself.

prerequisites: Admin access to the inherited account
steps: Open settings and list every feature actually available on the account.
Compare that list against what the current plan name should include.
Flag any mismatch to the owner before building on top of it.

test.method: Re-check the feature list once more after any plan change.
test.read_point: Before any build work starts on an inherited account

title: Read trial terms live and add payment before the promo window closes
hypothesis: If we read the current trial terms live and add payment details inside the stated window, then the promo trial stays intact because the terms differ by offer and go stale fast.

signal.check: A promo trial is being used and payment details have not been added inside the stated window.

expected_effect.size: unknown, terms vary and need a same-day web check

risk.note: Missing the window just means paying full price sooner, not losing the account.

steps: Check the current trial terms live on the day of signup, not from an old video or article.
Note the exact deadline to add payment details.
Add payment details before that deadline if the promo is worth keeping.

test.method: Confirm the promo rate is still applied on the first invoice.

title: Set currency, region, and units once, before entering any price
hypothesis: If we set store currency, backup region, and unit system once before entering prices, then repricing work is avoided because currency changes do not convert prices and unit changes mean converting every product.

signal.check: Products or prices are being entered before currency, region, and units are locked in.

risk.note: Changing currency later does not auto convert existing prices, and changing units means redoing every product.

prerequisites: Base currency, backup region, and unit system decided with the brand
steps: Confirm the target market's expected currency and unit system with the brand.
Set store currency, backup region, and unit system in settings.
Only then start entering product prices, weights, and dimensions.

test.method: Spot check 5 products for currency and unit consistency before launch.

title: Clean a fresh WordPress install before any product or theme work
hypothesis: If we deactivate and delete host bundled plugins, trash default content, and set core settings before any import, then storefront breakage drops because a leftover plugin can conflict with the starter site import.

signal.check: A fresh WordPress install exists with host bundled plugins, default pages, or extra themes still present.

risk.note: Take a backup first in case a needed setting gets removed by mistake.

prerequisites: A fresh WordPress install
A backup taken before cleanup
steps: Take a backup of the fresh install.
Deactivate then delete every host bundled plugin, keeping a host supplied caching plugin if present.
Trash default pages and posts, and delete all but one theme.
Set permalinks to Post name, timezone, and default new user role to Subscriber.
Disable comments if the storefront has no blog.

test.method: Re-check plugin and theme list right before the starter site import.

title: Write the site title and tagline to tell shoppers what and where you sell
hypothesis: If we write the site title and tagline as clear positioning, not an SEO trick, then first impression clarity improves because a shopper reads what the store sells and where it ships before anything else.

signal.check: The site title or tagline is generic, keyword stuffed, or does not say what the store sells and ships.

risk.note: Text can be edited any time.

steps: Write one line stating what the store sells and which countries it ships to.
Use that line as the site title or tagline, not a keyword list.
Route deeper SEO tactics to the SEO track instead of this field.

test.method: Read the title and tagline aloud and check a stranger understands the offer in one read.

title: Keep the store gated until the launch checklist passes
hypothesis: If we keep the storefront password protected or in coming soon until the pre-launch checklist passes, then first-visit trust improves because no shopper ever sees a half built store.

signal.check: The storefront is public or discoverable before the pre-launch checklist has passed.

risk.note: Gating can be turned on or off any time before launch.

steps: Turn on password protection (Shopify) or Coming soon (WooCommerce) at the start of the build.
Keep it on through every setup step.
Only remove it once the pre-launch checklist passes and the owner approves.

test.method: Confirm the storefront is not indexed or publicly reachable before the checklist passes.
test.read_point: Throughout the build, checked before launch

title: Buy or connect the domain to match the brand's registrar preference
hypothesis: If we buy through the platform for a simple connection or connect an existing domain when the brand already owns one, then setup time drops and the brand keeps the registrar control it wants.

signal.check: The brand has not decided whether to buy a new domain through the platform or connect one it already owns.

risk.note: The primary domain can be changed later, though DNS changes take time to propagate.

prerequisites: Domain decision made with the brand (registrar preference)
steps: Ask the brand whether it wants a new domain bought through the platform or an existing one connected.
For a platform purchase, search and buy; it auto connects with no DNS work.
For an existing domain, add the roughly 3 DNS records or nameserver change the platform shows, at the registrar.
Set the connected domain as primary once it resolves.

test.method: Load the domain in an incognito window and confirm it resolves to the store.

title: Reuse the DNS record workflow for sender and account domain verification
hypothesis: If we reuse the registrar DNS record workflow for email sender verification and a branded customer accounts domain, then email deliverability and brand consistency improve because both use the same record steps as the store domain.

signal.check: An ESP sender domain or branded customer accounts domain has not been authenticated yet.

expected_effect.size: unknown, authentication can take up to 48 hours

risk.note: DNS records can be removed if the setup needs to be undone.

prerequisites: Registrar access
ESP or customer accounts domain to authenticate
steps: Open the DNS record steps the ESP or platform shows for sender or accounts domain verification.
Add each record at the registrar under Manage DNS.
Wait up to 48 hours and confirm the status shows verified.

test.method: Send a test email through the ESP and check it is not flagged as unauthenticated.

title: Prepare brand assets before opening the theme editor
hypothesis: If we prepare the transparent logo, favicon, hex colors, fonts, and photos before opening the theme editor, then build speed improves because every field has a ready asset instead of a placeholder.

signal.check: Theme editing is starting without a finished logo, favicon, color palette, fonts, or product photos on hand.

risk.note: Assets can be swapped later, but doing so means redoing theme settings that reference them.

prerequisites: Brand assets from the brand track: logo, favicon, palette, fonts, photos
steps: Collect a transparent PNG logo and a square favicon, about 200 to 300 px wide.
Collect 4 to 5 hex colors with light and dark values.
Pick 1 to 2 fonts from the platform's font library.
Collect product and lifestyle photos and draft About page copy.
Only then open the theme editor.

test.method: Check no placeholder logo, color, or font remains once the theme copy is built.

title: List required theme sections and features before browsing themes
hypothesis: If we list required sections and features before browsing themes, then a costly late rebuild is avoided because a section missing from the theme cannot be added later without custom work.

signal.check: Theme browsing is starting with no written list of required sections, catalog size fit, or features like swatches or a mega menu.

risk.note: This is a planning step, not a store change.

prerequisites: Rough catalog size and required feature list from the brand
steps: List required features: swatches, before and after slider, mega menu, RTL, or anything the catalog needs.
Note the expected catalog size band, since themes filter by size roughly 11 to 100 versus 500 plus.
Use this list as the filter when browsing the theme store.

test.method: Check the chosen theme covers every item on the list before buying or committing.

title: Vet a theme on its product pages, mobile view, and developer, not the homepage
hypothesis: If we vet a shortlisted theme on its demo product pages, mobile preview, and developer track record, then post launch surprises drop because any feature shown in a demo preset is available across the whole theme.

signal.check: A theme is being shortlisted from its homepage screenshot alone, with no check of product pages, mobile view, or developer.

risk.note: This is a check step before committing to a theme.

prerequisites: Theme feature list (SET-019)
steps: Open the theme's own demo store, not just its screenshot.
Check the product page layout and features against the required list.
Check the mobile preview on a real phone size.
Check the developer's track record and update history before choosing.

test.method: Recheck the same 3 points after any major theme version update.
test.read_point: Before purchase and after any major theme update

title: Use an order ID prefix so competitors cannot read your order volume
hypothesis: If we add an order ID prefix or suffix, then a competitor or curious shopper cannot infer real order volume because the confirmation number no longer starts at a low, obviously new count.

signal.check: Order confirmation numbers are the plain default sequence, and the brand does not want order volume visible.

risk.note: The prefix can be changed later without affecting past orders.

steps: Decide if the brand wants order volume hidden from customers.
Add a prefix or suffix to the order number format in settings.
Keep the checkout confirmation step on regardless.

test.method: Check a test order confirmation number does not read as a low sequential count.

title: Never launch on the default platform domain or a pending domain
hypothesis: If we confirm the custom domain resolves before removing the password, then shopper trust improves because a store launching on a default myshopify or host domain, or a domain still pending, reads as unfinished.

signal.check: Launch is planned while the domain still shows pending in admin, or the store is only reachable on its default platform address.

risk.note: DNS records can be corrected and re-checked before launch.

prerequisites: Domain connected per the domain setup idea
steps: Open the custom domain directly in an incognito browser window, not the admin status page.
Confirm it loads the store, not a DNS error or the default platform address.
Do not remove the password or go live until the custom domain resolves cleanly.

test.method: Load the custom domain from a device outside the office network.

title: Decide free vs paid theme from the required feature list, not habit
hypothesis: If we decide free versus paid theme from the required section list, then the store spends only on features it actually needs because most stores do not need a paid theme unless one required feature is paid only.

signal.check: A theme is being picked without first checking whether the required feature list is covered by a free option.

expected_effect.size: $100 to $400 one time if paid is skipped, per source claims, needs a web check

risk.note: A free theme can be swapped for a paid one later, though work already done needs redoing.

prerequisites: Required theme feature list (theme prep idea)
steps: Check the required feature list against free theme options first.
Pay only when a required feature is genuinely paid only.
Use a trial to confirm before buying.

test.method: Track whether the chosen theme, free or paid, covers every required feature after launch.

title: Use the full theme trial to build before buying a paid theme
hypothesis: If we install a paid theme's full trial and build on it before buying, then wasted spend drops because buying only preserves work already tested, not a guess.

signal.check: A paid theme is being bought before its trial has been used to confirm fit.

risk.note: Trial work is lost only if the theme is never purchased.

steps: Click Try theme on the shortlisted paid theme.
Build the initial setup on the trial copy.
Buy only once the trial has proven the theme fits.

test.method: Confirm the paid purchase happens after, not before, the trial build.

title: Duplicate the theme before every edit, never touch the live theme
hypothesis: If we duplicate the theme before any major edit, update, or code change, then a bad edit never reaches shoppers because the live theme stays untouched until the copy is reviewed and published.

signal.check: Theme edits are being made directly on the live, published theme instead of a duplicate.

risk.note: The live theme stays safe as long as the duplicate rule is followed every round.

steps: Open the theme library and duplicate the current theme before starting any edit.
Rename the copy with today's date.
Work only on the copy.
Publish the copy only after review, then duplicate the now live theme again for the next round.

test.method: Check the theme library always shows a live theme and an untouched duplicate before any edit session.

title: Do not treat the one-click AI store generator as the final storefront
hypothesis: If we treat the one-click AI whole-store generator output as a rough starting idea rather than a finished storefront, then launch quality improves because the raw output is not reliable enough to ship as is.

signal.check: The AI whole-store generator's output is being prepared for launch without a manual design pass.

expected_effect.size: unknown, one source reverted to a standard theme after trying it

risk.note: Reverting to a standard theme is straightforward if the generated one underperforms.

steps: Use the generator only as a rough starting idea, not a final build.
Route detailed section and layout design to the landing page track.
Get a manual design and QA pass before launch.

test.method: Compare conversion on the generated storefront against a manually built one for a similar catalog.

title: Set brand colors once in theme settings and connect fields to them
hypothesis: If we set brand colors once in Settings and connect every theme field to them as a dynamic source, then future color changes take minutes because one update cascades everywhere instead of editing each section by hand.

signal.check: Theme sections use hard coded colors instead of a dynamic source linked to the saved brand palette.

risk.note: Colors can be relinked at any time.

prerequisites: Brand hex colors approved
steps: Enter the brand's hex colors once in Settings > Brand.
Open each theme color field and connect it to the saved brand color via the dynamic source icon.
Prefer theme level custom CSS over editing individual theme files.

test.method: Change one brand color and confirm it cascades across the storefront without manual edits.
test.read_point: Any time a brand color changes

title: Remove all demo content and default text before launch
hypothesis: If we remove demo products, demo categories, and default store name text before launch, then shopper trust improves because nothing on the live site reads as an unfinished template.

signal.check: Demo products, demo categories, a demo store notice, or a default footer store name are still visible on the storefront.

risk.note: Removing demo content does not affect any real data.

steps: Delete demo products and demo categories.
Remove any demo store notice and Powered by text where the plan allows.
Set the real store name in Settings > General so the footer no longer reads the theme's default name.

test.method: Browse the full live storefront and footer looking for any leftover demo or default text.

title: Lock the page builder choice once, and pin plugin versions if unstable
hypothesis: If we choose the page builder deliberately at starter site import and pin plugin versions when a new major release is unstable, then rebuild risk drops because the builder choice locks the editor for every later page.

signal.check: A starter site is being imported without a deliberate page builder choice, or a newly released plugin major version is reported unstable.

risk.note: Switching page builders after pages are built means rebuilding every page.

steps: Choose Elementor or the block editor deliberately before the starter site import.
Check current release notes for the builder plugin before updating.
Pin the plugin to the last stable version if a new major release is reported unstable.

test.method: Check the site after any plugin update for broken layouts before publishing the update.
test.read_point: Before and after any builder plugin update

title: Match each product's type to how it is really sold and fulfilled
hypothesis: If we pick the product type that matches how an item is sold and fulfilled, then shipping and tax errors drop because a physical item marked digital or downloadable skips shipping and tax by mistake.

signal.check: A physical product is set up as virtual, downloadable, or with the weight toggle off, or a digital item is set up as physical.

risk.note: A wrong product type found before launch is a quick fix; found after real orders it means refunds and re-shipping.

prerequisites: Product catalog with fulfilment method per SKU
steps: List each product's real fulfilment method: physical, virtual service, downloadable file, or external listing.
Set the matching product type on the platform for every SKU.
Check no physical item is marked digital or downloadable.

test.method: Place a test order on every distinct product type and confirm shipping and tax behave correctly.

title: Turn on the physical weight toggle and enter a weight for every shippable product
hypothesis: If we turn on the physical weight toggle and enter a weight for every shippable product, even on flat rates, then future shipping switches and warehouse integrations work because the toggle being off treats the item as digital with no shipping at checkout.
does_not_apply_when: Product is genuinely digital with no shipping

signal.check: A shippable product has the physical weight toggle off or no weight entered.

risk.note: Weight can be added or corrected at any time.

prerequisites: Per-product weight data
steps: Turn on the physical product toggle for every shippable product.
Enter a weight for every shippable product, even on flat rate shipping.
Do this even if the store currently uses flat rates only, in case rates change later.

test.method: Spot check 10 products for the physical toggle and a non-zero weight.

title: Enter outer package weight and dimensions, not the bare product
hypothesis: If we enter the outer package weight and dimensions instead of the bare product weight, then shipping quotes stop running light because calculated and weight based rates undercharge without the packaging weight included.
does_not_apply_when: Store uses only flat per-order shipping rates that never scale with weight

signal.check: Shipping rates are calculated or weight based, but products only carry the bare item weight, not the packaged weight.

risk.note: Package weight can be corrected any time.

prerequisites: Package weight and dimensions per product or per package type
steps: Weigh the item as it will actually ship, in its box or mailer, not just the bare product.
Enter that packaged weight and dimensions on the product or the assigned package.
Repeat for every product on calculated, weight, or class based rates.

test.method: Quote a shipping rate before and after setting the package weight and confirm the quote rises.

title: Launch with fewer complete products instead of a full catalog of thin ones
hypothesis: If we launch with fewer, fully complete products instead of padding the catalog with thin listings, then buy confidence improves because every listed product actually has the depth a shopper needs to decide.

signal.check: The launch catalog includes several products with missing photos, thin descriptions, or unset fields, added just to raise product count.

risk.note: More products can be added after launch once they are complete.

steps: List every product that currently passes the product data completeness checklist.
Hold back any product missing photos, pricing, or description depth.
Launch with only the complete set, however small.

test.method: Compare add to cart rate on complete versus thin listings once both types have run.

title: Complete every required field on every product before publishing
hypothesis: If we fill title, descriptions, media, type, vendor, tags, category, pricing, cost, SKU, stock, weight, and SEO fields on every product, then buy confidence improves because the shopper has everything needed to decide.

signal.check: Products are live with missing short description, media, type, tags, cost, SKU, or SEO title and meta.

risk.note: Fields can be edited any time, though a title change means the URL handle needs fixing too.

prerequisites: Product import sheet with all fields filled
steps: Write a specific title and a short description above the buy area for every product.
Add a long description below it, never copied from a supplier.
Upload media in one consistent ratio, at least 1000 by 1000 px, clearest image first.
Fill type, vendor, tags, category, price, compare-at only if real, and cost per item.
Fill SEO title and meta description.
Set status to Active only once every field above is filled.

test.method: Run the product completeness checklist against every SKU before launch.

title: Fix the product URL handle whenever a product is retitled
hypothesis: If we update the product URL handle every time a product is retitled, then broken links and lost search rankings are avoided because the handle does not update automatically to match a new title.

signal.check: A product has been retitled but its URL handle still reflects the old name.

risk.note: Changing the handle after it has been indexed or linked needs a redirect to avoid a broken link.

steps: After retitling a product, open its SEO or URL handle field.
Update the handle to match the new title.
If the old handle was already public, add a redirect from the old URL to the new one.

test.method: Spot check that every product's handle matches its current title.

title: Keep compare-at prices real and schedule every sale to end
hypothesis: If we only use a compare-at price that was a real former price and schedule every sale to end, then shopper trust holds because an overstated or permanent discount costs credibility once noticed.

signal.check: A compare-at or sale price shows a discount with no real former price, or a sale has no end date.

risk.note: A WooCommerce sale price with no end date never reverts on its own.

prerequisites: Real historical prices per product
steps: Only enter a compare-at price that was actually charged before.
Set an end date on every scheduled sale price.
Check regularly that no sale has run past its intended end date.

test.method: Audit active discounts monthly for real former prices and expired end dates.

title: Enter cost per item on every product so margin reports work
hypothesis: If we enter the cost of goods per item on every product, then margin reporting becomes usable because the platform can only calculate profit once real cost data is present.

signal.check: Products are live with an empty cost per item field.

expected_effect.size: unknown, this only unlocks the reporting, it does not change actual margin

risk.note: Cost can be edited any time; wrong cost just means wrong reports until fixed.

prerequisites: Cost of goods per SKU from the sourcing record
steps: Pull cost of goods per SKU from the sourcing or import sheet.
Enter it in the cost per item field on every product.
Recheck after any supplier price change.

test.method: Pull a margin report and confirm no product shows a blank or zero cost.
test.read_point: Before launch, and after any price change

title: Turn on inventory tracking and give every product a SKU or barcode
hypothesis: If we turn on inventory tracking and assign a SKU or barcode to every product, even when dropshipping, then fulfilment accuracy improves because the warehouse needs one to match what was ordered.

signal.check: Products are live with tracking off, or missing or duplicated SKUs.

risk.note: SKUs and tracking can be added at any time.

prerequisites: A SKU naming convention agreed with the brand
steps: Agree a SKU convention: lowercase title, hyphens, a running number or variant suffix.
Turn on inventory tracking for every product.
Assign a unique SKU or barcode to every product and variant, even dropshipped ones.
Use a real UPC or GTIN only if the brand owns one.

test.method: Check for duplicate or missing SKUs across the full catalog.

title: Set continue-selling and backorder rules by real fulfilment ability
hypothesis: If we turn continue-selling on only when the brand can source after the sale and off for fixed stock, then oversold orders drop because the setting no longer promises stock the brand cannot deliver.

signal.check: Continue-selling is on for a product with fixed physical stock and no fast restock path, or off for a dropship item that could keep selling.

risk.note: Getting this wrong leads to overselling, which costs a refund and an apology.

prerequisites: Real fulfilment ability per SKU (dropship vs fixed stock)
steps: Mark each product as dropship or fixed stock.
Turn continue-selling on only for dropship items the brand can still source.
Turn continue-selling off for fixed stock items so they show sold out at zero.
Set a low stock threshold to trigger restocking before hitting zero.
Allow backorders only where a fast restock path exists.

test.method: Check no fixed stock product shows continue-selling on after zero units sold.

title: Confirm real supplier stock separately from the inventory number shown
hypothesis: If we confirm real supplier or fulfilment stock separately from the platform's inventory number, then overselling drops because setting a high inventory number only stops sold out messages, it does not create real stock.

signal.check: A product's inventory number is set high to avoid a sold out message, with no separate check of real supplier stock.

risk.note: Selling against phantom stock leads to cancellations and refunds.

prerequisites: A direct line to the supplier or fulfilment app's real stock count
steps: Check the supplier's or fulfilment app's real stock count, not just the platform's inventory number.
Reconcile the two numbers before launch.
Repeat the reconciliation on a set schedule after launch.

test.method: Compare platform inventory to supplier stock count for the top 10 SKUs.
test.read_point: Weekly in the first month, then monthly

title: Write original, benefit-led product descriptions, never copy supplier text
hypothesis: If we write original, benefit-led descriptions instead of pasting supplier copy, then conversion and search visibility improve because duplicate, generic text neither converts shoppers nor ranks well.

signal.check: A product description matches the supplier's or manufacturer's listing text word for word.

risk.note: Descriptions can be rewritten at any time.

steps: Check every product description against the supplier's original listing text.
Rewrite any matching description in the brand's own voice, leading with the benefit.
Keep the short description above the buy area and the long detail below it.

test.method: Run a duplicate content check against supplier listings after rewriting.

title: Set a low stock alert threshold so restocking starts before zero
hypothesis: If we set a low stock threshold on every tracked product, then stockouts drop because the brand gets a warning to reorder before the count hits zero.
does_not_apply_when: Product is made to order with no fixed stock to run low on

signal.check: Tracked products have no low stock threshold set, so restocking only happens after a sellout.

expected_effect.size: demo thresholds of 2, 3, or 10 units seen in sources, set from real lead time

risk.note: Threshold can be adjusted any time as lead times change.

prerequisites: Supplier lead time per SKU
steps: Get supplier lead time in days for each SKU.
Set a low stock threshold that gives enough runway to reorder before selling out.
Review thresholds after any change in supplier lead time or sell-through rate.

test.method: Track how often a SKU hits zero stock before a reorder is placed.

title: On Shopify, add variant options and price every single variant row
hypothesis: If we generate variant options with Add options and fill a price, image, and stock on every row, then add to cart failures drop because a variation with no price cannot be added to the cart.

signal.check: A Shopify product has variant options generated but one or more rows are missing a price, image, or stock count.

risk.note: Variant rows can be edited any time.

prerequisites: Per-variant price, image, and stock data
steps: Add the option types the product needs, such as Size and Color.
Generate the resulting variant rows.
Open every row and fill price, quantity, and an assigned image.
Set the default form values to match the default image shown.

test.method: Add every variant combination to cart on the live product and confirm none fail.

title: On WooCommerce, build variant options from global attributes, not product-level ones
hypothesis: If we build variant options from global attributes instead of product-level ones, then catalog filters and future edits work because global attributes are reusable and feed storefront filters, while product-level ones are not.

signal.check: Variable products are using product-level attributes instead of global attributes shared across the catalog.

risk.note: Migrating existing product-level attributes to global ones after the fact takes rework across every affected product.

prerequisites: List of shared attributes (Size, Color) across the catalog
steps: Create each shared attribute as a global attribute under Products > Attributes.
On each variable product, add the existing global attributes and mark them Used for variations.
Generate variations, then fill price, SKU, stock, and image on every row.
Set default form values to match the default image.

test.method: Confirm the storefront filter by attribute works across multiple products sharing it.

title: Verify color swatches are accurate and add hex values for patterns
hypothesis: If we verify auto-detected color swatches and add hex values or a label image for patterns, then returns for wrong color drop because auto-detected colors are close but not exact.

signal.check: Color swatches were auto-generated and have not been checked against the real product color, or a patterned variant has no label image.

risk.note: Swatches can be corrected any time.

prerequisites: Real product color reference photos
steps: Compare every auto-detected swatch color against the real product photo.
Correct any hex value that does not match.
Add a label image for any pattern that a plain swatch cannot represent.
Group variant images so selecting a swatch shows the matching photo, if the theme supports it.

test.method: Check swatch colors against real product photos for the top selling variants.

title: Decide collections first, then tag to match, and copy-paste every tag
hypothesis: If we decide the collection plan first, then tag every product by copy-pasting from that plan, then a smart collection or filter never silently breaks because a typo like bras versus browse or legging versus leggings fragments the results.

signal.check: Products are being tagged freehand rather than from a fixed collection and tag plan.

risk.note: Tags can be bulk edited to fix typos once found.

prerequisites: Written collection and tag plan
steps: Write the full collection plan and its exact tag list before tagging any product.
Copy and paste tags from that list onto every product, never retype them.
Spot check smart collections and filters for a product that should appear but does not.

test.method: Check every smart collection shows the expected product count against the plan.

title: Use bulk edit or import, and duplicate configured products, for a large catalog
hypothesis: If we use bulk edit or import for a large catalog and duplicate a fully configured product to speed up similar ones, then build time drops because every field does not need re-entry from scratch.

signal.check: A catalog with many similar products is being built one product at a time with no bulk edit, import, or duplication.

risk.note: Bulk edits can be reversed by re-editing the affected fields.

prerequisites: One fully configured reference product per product family
steps: Fully configure one reference product per family first.
Duplicate it for each similar product and scrub every field that differs.
Use bulk edit for shared field changes across many products at once.
Move to a dedicated import or bulk edit app once the built-in bulk edit hits its limits.

test.method: Time how long it takes to add 10 similar products with duplication versus from scratch.

title: Set upsells and cross-sells deliberately once target products exist
hypothesis: If we set product page upsells and cart cross-sells deliberately after the target products already exist, then average order value has a real lever to test because the mechanism is in place to try and measure.

signal.check: Products have no upsell or cross-sell set, or one was set before the target product existed.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no source measures lift, mechanism only

risk.note: Upsells and cross-sells can be changed any time.

prerequisites: A defined set of higher-margin or complementary products to promote
steps: Pick the product to promote as an upsell or cross-sell for each core item.
Set the upsell on the product page and the cross-sell in the cart.
Track add-on attach rate once live and adjust the pairing if it underperforms.

test.method: Track attach rate and AOV lift on orders where the upsell or cross-sell is shown versus not.

title: Set a catalog placeholder image and keep every product image the same size
hypothesis: If we set a catalog placeholder image and keep all product images at the same width and height, then the collection grid stops misaligning because mixed ratios force the theme to crop images awkwardly.

signal.check: Product images vary in width to height ratio across the catalog, or no placeholder image is set for products with none yet.

risk.note: Images can be re-uploaded any time.

prerequisites: A fixed image ratio for the catalog
steps: Pick one fixed image ratio for the whole catalog.
Upload a placeholder image on WooCommerce for any product missing a photo.
Re-crop or re-shoot any product image that does not match the fixed ratio.

test.method: Browse the full collection grid and check for misaligned or cropped cards.

title: Set digital product download limits and expiry, then test the download
hypothesis: If we set a deliberate download limit and expiry and test the download after a real purchase, then digital fulfilment tickets drop because a broken or missing download link is never found by a customer first.

signal.check: A digital product has default or unset download limit and expiry, or has never been test-purchased.

risk.note: Limits and expiry can be changed any time.

prerequisites: The final digital file uploaded
steps: Decide a download limit and expiry that fits the product, unlimited or a set number of days.
Set stock tracking off but still set a SKU for reporting.
Place a real test purchase and confirm the download works end to end.

test.method: Complete a real test purchase and download the file.

title: Set up gift cards correctly for digital auto-fulfil versus a physical card
hypothesis: If we treat gift cards as digital and auto-fulfilled by default and set up a physical card as a separate manual add-on, then gift card orders stop stalling because the platform's default handling only covers the digital path.

signal.check: The brand sells or plans to sell gift cards, physical, digital, or both, with no clear setup for each.

risk.note: Gift card settings can be adjusted any time.

prerequisites: Decision on whether to offer digital, physical, or both gift card types
steps: Confirm the digital gift card product auto-fulfils by email on purchase.
If a physical card is offered, set it up as a manual add-on product with its own fulfilment step.
Test purchase both types before launch if both are offered.

test.method: Place a test purchase of each gift card type and confirm delivery.

title: Decide manual versus smart collection type with growth in mind
hypothesis: If we decide manual versus smart collection type deliberately before saving, then future upkeep drops because the type cannot be changed after save and a manual collection needs every new product added by hand.
does_not_apply_when: Store has a single hero SKU with no real collection structure needed

signal.check: A collection is about to be saved without a deliberate decision on manual versus smart type, or the catalog is growing and still relies on manual collections.

risk.note: The collection type is permanent on Shopify once saved; a wrong choice means recreating the collection.

prerequisites: Consistent product tags to support smart collections
steps: Default to a tag-based smart collection for a catalog expected to grow.
Use a manual collection only for a fixed, curated set that will not need every new product added.
Confirm the tag plan is consistent enough to support the smart collection's conditions before saving.

test.method: Check no growing collection is still manual and unfed 3 months after launch.

title: Choose smart collection conditions deliberately: any to pool, all to intersect
hypothesis: If we choose any to pool sub-groups into a parent collection and all to intersect narrower conditions, then collections show the right products because the match logic matches shopper intent instead of a default guess.

signal.check: A smart collection is being built without a deliberate choice between any and all match logic.

risk.note: Conditions can be edited without recreating the collection.

prerequisites: Collection plan with intended product membership
steps: Decide if the collection should pool several sub-groups (use any) or narrow by several conditions at once (use all).
Add conditions from price, inventory level, category, vendor, or weight as needed.
Check the resulting product list matches intent before publishing.

test.method: Compare the collection's actual product list to the intended list from the plan.

title: Delete or rename default collections and categories before launch
hypothesis: If we delete an unused default collection or rename an undeletable default category, then navigation reads as intentional because no shopper hits a generic Home page collection or an unrenamed Uncategorized category.

signal.check: A default collection or category with a generic platform name is still live and unused.

risk.note: Renaming is fully reversible; deleting a Shopify default collection is not needed elsewhere.

steps: On Shopify, delete the default Home page collection if it is unused.
On WooCommerce, rename the undeletable default category to a real category name.
Check no navigation link still points at the old default.

test.method: Browse collections and categories for any generic default name still live.

title: Build menus around how shoppers think, reachable in 2 to 3 clicks
hypothesis: If we build the main menu around how shoppers categorize products and keep every product reachable in 2 to 3 clicks, then browse-to-product conversion improves because shoppers find what they want faster.

signal.check: The main menu is built around internal team names, or a product needs more than 3 clicks to reach from the homepage.

expected_effect.size: unknown, 2 to 3 clicks is a stated heuristic

risk.note: Menus can be rebuilt any time.

prerequisites: Collection plan finalized
steps: List how a shopper would naturally search for the catalog, not how the team organizes it internally.
Build the menu around that list, nesting up to 3 levels for a mega menu.
Support more than one path to the same product where it makes sense.
Remove default links that add no shopping path.
Click through from the homepage to confirm every product is reachable in 2 to 3 clicks.

test.method: Count the clicks from the homepage to a sample of 10 products.

title: Build footer legal and quick-link menus only after the pages exist
hypothesis: If we build the footer's legal and quick-link menus in the backend after the linked pages are published, then the footer stops showing dead links because an unpublished page has no URL to link.

signal.check: Footer menu items point at policy or info pages that are not yet published.

risk.note: Footer menus can be rebuilt any time.

prerequisites: All legal and info pages published
steps: Publish every legal and info page first.
Build a Legal or Helpful Links menu and a Quick Links menu in the backend pointing at those pages.
Assign the menus to the footer blocks.
Click every footer link in an incognito window to confirm none is dead.

test.method: Click every footer link in an incognito window.

title: Install Search and Discovery for filters, and fill the fields filters need
hypothesis: If we install the free Search and Discovery app and fill the underlying fields on every product, then filters and search results stop showing gaps because a filter only shows options for fields that are actually filled in.

signal.check: A storefront filter shows only one value or an incomplete list because the underlying product field is not filled on every product.

risk.note: Filters and their fields can be adjusted any time.

prerequisites: Product metafields or standard fields needed for filters
steps: Install the free Search and Discovery app.
Pick the filters that matter: availability, price, and any relevant category or custom metafield.
Fill that field on every product in the catalog, not just a few.
Uninstall any paid app doing the same job.

test.method: Test each filter and confirm it returns every product that should match.

title: Create every required legal and info page before launch
hypothesis: If we create About, Contact, shipping, return, privacy, and terms pages before launch, then footer links resolve and shopper trust holds because a footer link to a missing policy does not render.

signal.check: Any of About, Contact, shipping, return, privacy, or terms pages does not exist yet, and launch is approaching.

risk.note: Pages can be edited after launch, but should exist before it.

prerequisites: Draft content or a template for each page
steps: List the 6 required pages: About, Contact, shipping, return and refund, privacy, and terms.
Draft each one, using the platform template as a starting point where one exists.
Publish all 6 before linking any of them in the footer or navigation.

test.method: Confirm all 6 pages are published and reachable before building footer links.

title: Edit every placeholder in a policy template before publishing it
hypothesis: If we insert the platform's policy template then edit every placeholder and clause to match real practice, then legal exposure drops because publishing a template unmodified has left brackets like insert return address live before.

signal.check: A policy page still contains template placeholders such as brackets or generic instructional text.

risk.note: An unedited placeholder in a live legal page is a real dispute and refund risk until fixed.

prerequisites: Real shipping, return, privacy, and terms practices documented
steps: Insert the platform's template for privacy, terms, and refund and return policies.
Write the shipping policy from scratch, since Shopify has no template for it.
Replace every placeholder and bracket with real brand information.
Read the whole page once more before publishing, looking only for leftover placeholders.

test.method: Read the first paragraph of every policy in an incognito window for placeholders.

title: Get a human legal sign-off on AI-drafted shipping, return, privacy, and terms text
hypothesis: If we treat AI-drafted legal pages as a first pass only and get a human with legal knowledge to sign off before they govern a real order, then chargeback and refund disputes are handled on solid ground because the pages reflect a real legal review, not just a draft.

signal.check: Shipping, return, privacy, or terms pages were AI-drafted and have not had a human legal review recorded.

risk.note: Governing a real order or refund on unreviewed legal text is the actual risk this closes.

prerequisites: AI draft of each legal page
Access to someone with legal knowledge for the brand's markets
steps: Draft each legal page with a clear brief: what is sold, to which countries, and which pages are needed.
Send every draft to a human with legal knowledge, especially for the EU, UK, or UAE.
Record the reviewer's name and date on the launch checklist.
Do not treat any legal page as final until this sign-off is recorded.

test.method: Check the launch checklist for a recorded legal sign-off name and date.

title: Write real shipping terms with a cross-border duties disclosure
hypothesis: If we write real delivery windows, handling time, and a visible duties note for US and Canada bound cross-border orders, then support tickets and disputes drop because a thin shipping policy is a named driver of both.

signal.check: The shipping policy is generic or missing delivery windows, handling time, or a cross-border duties note.

risk.note: The shipping policy text does not set checkout rates; those live in shipping settings separately.

prerequisites: Real delivery windows and handling times from fulfilment
steps: Write real delivery windows and handling time based on actual fulfilment capability.
State the conditions clearly: which countries, which methods, and any exceptions.
Add a visible note for US and Canada bound cross-border orders that import duties may apply.
Keep this policy in sync with the actual checkout shipping rates.

test.method: Read the shipping policy against the actual configured rates for a mismatch.

title: Configure return rules and enable self-serve returns after the policy is published
hypothesis: If we configure the return window, who pays return shipping, restocking fee, and final sale items, then enable self-serve returns, then post-purchase tickets drop because customers can act on clear, published rules instead of emailing to ask.

signal.check: Return rules are not fully configured, or self-serve returns is off despite a published return policy.

risk.note: Return rules can be adjusted any time.

prerequisites: Return policy published
steps: Set the return window, who pays return shipping, restocking fee if any, and final sale item list.
Publish the return policy with these exact terms.
Enable self-serve returns once the policy matches the configured rules.

test.method: Run a test self-serve return request and confirm it follows the published rules.

title: Point the checkout agree-box at the real Terms page, never a borrowed one
hypothesis: If we replace any borrowed page standing in for Terms and Conditions at the checkout agree-box with the real page, then the store has an enforceable return contract because a shopper who agreed to the wrong terms has none.

signal.check: The checkout agree-box links to a Privacy page or another borrowed page instead of the real Terms and Conditions page.

risk.note: Every order placed while the wrong page is linked has no enforceable terms contract.

prerequisites: Real Terms and Conditions page published
steps: Publish the real Terms and Conditions page.
Open the checkout settings and find the read and agree box configuration.
Point it at the real Terms page, not Privacy or any other borrowed page.
Place a test order and confirm the agree-box link opens the correct page.

test.method: Click the checkout agree-box link on a test order and confirm it opens the real Terms page.

title: Have a working support channel live before the first order
hypothesis: If we confirm a working contact channel before the first order ships, then response time holds because a new store gets support emails about sizing, shipping, and order status from day one.

signal.check: The support email or contact form has not been tested end to end before launch.

risk.note: Contact channels can be fixed quickly if a test reveals a bounce.

prerequisites: Support email and contact form set up
steps: Send a test message through the contact form and to the support email.
Confirm someone receives and can reply to both.
Set expectations with the team that support emails start on day one.

test.method: Send a test message and time the reply.

title: Close cookie consent, data privacy, and accessibility gaps with human review
hypothesis: If we add cookie consent, GDPR and CCPA data handling copy, and an accessibility pass with a human review, then legal exposure drops because no source in this playbook covers these steps in detail.

signal.check: The store has no cookie consent banner, no GDPR or CCPA data handling statement, and no accessibility check has been done.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no library source covers this in detail

risk.note: These are named gaps across every source; skipping them leaves real legal exposure in regulated markets.

prerequisites: Target market list to know which laws apply
steps: Confirm which target markets require cookie consent, GDPR, or CCPA style disclosures.
Install a cookie consent solution and write the data handling disclosure with human legal input.
Run a basic accessibility pass on the storefront (contrast, alt text, keyboard navigation).
Route deeper security and accessibility hardening to the dedicated security folder.

test.method: Run a compliance checklist against each target market's requirements.

title: Turn on two-factor authentication before activating payments
hypothesis: If we turn on two-factor authentication before activating the payments account, then payout theft risk drops because the account protects real payout money, not just content.

signal.check: Payments are being activated on an account with two-factor authentication still off.

risk.note: Two-factor can be enabled at any time, though it should happen before payments, not after.

steps: Open account security settings and turn on two-step authentication.
Save recovery codes in the brand's secret store, never a notes app.
Only then activate the payments account.

test.method: Confirm two-factor shows on before opening the payments activation flow.

title: Match identity documents exactly when verifying payments
hypothesis: If we enter names, addresses, and IDs in payments setup exactly as they appear on government and registration documents, then verification holds go down because a mismatch is the stated top cause of a verification hold.

signal.check: Payments verification is being submitted with a nickname, shortened name, or an address that does not exactly match official documents.

risk.note: A mismatch found after submission means a re-review that costs days.

prerequisites: Government ID and business registration documents on hand
steps: Choose Individual or Business as the correct account type.
Enter the exact legal name and address as shown on the ID or registration document.
Confirm the payout bank account accepts the correct regional deposit type.
Submit and expect a review that can take hours to days; keep building meanwhile.

test.method: Compare every entered field character by character against the source document before submitting.

title: Add a second payment method alongside the primary gateway
hypothesis: If we add PayPal or another second payment method alongside the primary gateway, then checkout completion improves because relying on one payment method is a named beginner mistake that loses shoppers who prefer another option.

signal.check: Checkout offers only one payment method.

risk.note: A payment method can be removed if it underperforms.

prerequisites: Gateway availability checked for the brand's country
steps: Check which gateways are available in the brand's country.
Set the primary gateway as the default where currency and wallet support are strongest.
Add PayPal, or Stripe if the primary is unavailable, as a second option.
Place a test order through each method before launch.

test.method: Track checkout completion rate before and after the second method goes live.

title: Add well-known regional payment methods for key markets
hypothesis: If we add regional payment methods shoppers already expect, such as buy-now-pay-later in the UK or cash on delivery where it is common, then checkout completion improves in that market because the store meets a local habit instead of forcing an unfamiliar one.

signal.check: The store sells into a market with a well-known regional payment preference that is not yet offered at checkout.

expected_effect.size: unknown, names need a web check

risk.note: A regional method can be removed if uptake is low.

prerequisites: Web check on current regional payment method names and eligibility
steps: Identify which regional payment method shoppers in each key market expect.
Web check current availability and eligibility for that method.
Enable it at checkout for that market only.
Track uptake and remove it if usage stays negligible.

test.method: Track the share of orders in that market using the regional method.

title: Set payment capture to automatic unless orders are reviewed before charging
hypothesis: If we set payment capture to automatic at checkout unless the brand deliberately reviews orders first, then cash flow and order processing speed improve because funds and fulfilment start moving without a manual capture step.
does_not_apply_when: Brand deliberately reviews every order for fraud or customization before charging

signal.check: Payment capture is set to manual with no deliberate reason to review orders before charging.

risk.note: Capture setting can be changed any time.

steps: Decide if orders genuinely need manual review before charging.
If not, set payment capture to automatic at checkout.
Keep wallet buttons like Shop Pay, Apple Pay, and Google Pay on regardless.

test.method: Check the time from order placed to payment captured over a week of orders.

title: Use dedicated, matched gateway plugins on WooCommerce with a real PayPal Business account
hypothesis: If we install dedicated Stripe and PayPal plugins matching the publisher exactly and require a real PayPal Business account, then checkout failures drop because a mismatched plugin publisher or a personal PayPal account both cause processing problems.

signal.check: A Stripe or PayPal plugin is installed from a publisher that does not match the one being configured, or PayPal is connected with a personal account.

risk.note: Switching plugins later means reconnecting and re-testing the gateway.

prerequisites: A PayPal Business account
A Stripe account
steps: Pick one Stripe plugin and one PayPal plugin, matching the publisher name exactly.
Upgrade any personal PayPal account to a Business account before connecting.
Set the statement descriptor to the company name.
Order payment methods with card above PayPal at checkout.

test.method: Place a full sandbox order through each gateway plugin.

title: Test every gateway in sandbox, then place one small live order and refund it
hypothesis: If we connect every gateway in test mode, place a full test order, switch to live, then place and refund one small real order, then checkout failures at launch drop because keys pasted in the wrong mode fail silently and a gateway can deactivate for incomplete verification.

signal.check: A gateway has been connected but never run through a full test order in sandbox and a real order in live mode.

risk.note: A failed live test before launch is far cheaper to fix than one found on the first real customer order.

prerequisites: Test card numbers for the gateway
steps: Connect the gateway in test or sandbox mode.
Place a full test order using the gateway's own test card.
Confirm the connection test reads Live before switching modes.
Switch to live and place one small real order, then refund it from the order screen.

test.method: Confirm the refund appears in the gateway dashboard after the live test order.

title: Keep every payment key out of files, prompts, and chat
hypothesis: If we keep Stripe, PayPal, and gateway keys out of files, prompts, and chat, and have a human paste them directly in the platform UI, then a leaked key can never move real customer payments or take checkout down.

signal.check: A payment key, secret, or test card number has appeared in a document, prompt, or chat instead of being pasted directly by a human into the platform UI.

risk.note: If a key is ever exposed, rotate it immediately rather than leaving it live.

steps: Never paste a Stripe, PayPal, or gateway key into a file, prompt, or chat message.
Have a human enter keys directly in the platform UI.
Rotate any key that was ever exposed, even briefly.

test.method: Search recent files, prompts, and chat logs for any key or secret pattern.

title: Turn off test mode and remove the password only after the test order passes
hypothesis: If we turn test mode off and remove the password only after the test order passes, then no real sale is silently blocked because both settings left on stop every checkout attempt.

signal.check: Launch is planned while payment test mode is still on, or before a test order has passed cleanly.

risk.note: Leaving test mode on after removing the password means every real customer sale silently fails.

prerequisites: A passed test order (SET-072)
steps: Confirm the test order passed cleanly across tax, shipping, and email.
Turn off payment test mode.
Only then remove the storefront password or switch to Live.

test.method: Confirm test mode reads off and the storefront is public in the same session.

title: Turn on fraud screening and card verification at the gateway
hypothesis: If we turn on order risk scoring, address and card verification, and 3D Secure where a market mandates it, then chargeback losses drop because the gateway screens suspicious orders before they complete.

signal.check: The payment gateway has risk scoring, AVS, CVV, or 3D Secure available but not turned on.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no library source, verify against brand data

risk.note: Overly strict fraud rules can also block real customers, so monitor decline rates after enabling.

prerequisites: Gateway dashboard access
steps: Turn on order risk scoring in the gateway dashboard.
Turn on address and card verification (AVS, CVV).
Require 3D Secure or SCA for markets that mandate it, such as the EU.
Monitor decline rate for a false positive spike after enabling.

test.method: Track chargeback rate and false decline rate for 8 weeks after enabling.

title: Screen for fake COD orders and offer a prepaid discount to pull volume off COD
hypothesis: If we screen high cash-on-delivery orders for fake order patterns, verify the phone number, and offer a small prepaid discount, then failed and fraudulent COD deliveries drop because COD carries more return and non-payment risk than prepaid.
does_not_apply_when: Cash on delivery is not a meaningful share of orders

signal.check: Cash on delivery makes up a large share of orders with no phone verification or fake order screening in place.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no library source for the controls, verify against brand data

risk.note: Too aggressive screening can block real customers, so tune thresholds carefully.

prerequisites: Order and delivery data to identify fake order patterns
steps: Enable a phone verification step for COD orders.
Flag repeat-fail or suspicious address patterns for manual review.
Offer a small discount for prepaid orders to shift volume off COD.
Track COD failure rate before and after.

test.method: Track the share of COD orders that fail delivery or payment before and after the controls.

title: Re-check the payment gateway is still active right before removing the password
hypothesis: If we re-open the payments settings right before removing the password, then a silent launch failure is avoided because a gateway can deactivate later if verification data is incomplete, blocking every checkout with no obvious warning.

signal.check: Time has passed since payments were first verified, and the gateway has not been re-checked right before password removal.

risk.note: A deactivated gateway blocks all checkouts with no obvious storefront symptom until an order fails.

steps: Open payments settings again right before removing the password.
Confirm the gateway shows active, not paused for missing verification.
Only remove the password once this is confirmed.

test.method: Check the gateway status screen shows active immediately before launch.

title: Give every target country an explicit shipping rate
hypothesis: If we add an explicit shipping rate for every country the brand sells to, then checkout abandonment in that country drops because a country with no rate is marked unshippable and blocks the sale entirely.

signal.check: One or more target countries has no configured shipping rate, so products show as unshippable there.

risk.note: Rates can be added or edited any time.

prerequisites: List of every target country and its shipping cost
steps: List every country the brand sells and ships to.
Set selling locations and shipping locations to match that list.
Add a rate for every country on the list before launch.
Quote a test order to each country to confirm a rate shows.

test.method: Quote a test order to every target country and confirm none shows unshippable.

title: Start with a domestic flat rate, then add international zones as needed
hypothesis: If we start with a single domestic zone and flat rate, then add international zones only as needed, then setup complexity drops because shipping worldwide by default adds cost and complexity the brand may not need yet.

signal.check: Shipping is being configured for every country worldwide by default before international demand exists.

risk.note: Zones can be added at any time as international demand appears.

steps: Set up the domestic zone with one flat rate and one profile first.
Delete any rate option the brand will not honor, such as an unused express tier.
Add international zones and profiles only once there is real demand to serve.

test.method: Track international order requests before deciding to add a zone.

title: Review or replace default shipping zones and rates before launch
hypothesis: If we review or replace the platform's pre-created shipping zones, rates, and free threshold before launch, then real shipping costs stay covered because the default weight-based rates and threshold rarely match the brand's actual costs.

signal.check: The platform's default shipping zones and rates, including any default free shipping threshold, have not been reviewed since account creation.

risk.note: A left-in-place default rate can quietly undercharge shipping until noticed.

prerequisites: Real shipping cost matrix (rates, threshold, transit times)
steps: Open shipping settings and inspect every pre-created zone and rate.
Compare each against the brand's real shipping cost matrix.
Edit or delete any default that does not match, including the default free threshold.

test.method: Quote a default-zone order and check the rate matches the real cost matrix.

title: Set the free shipping threshold from the brand's own margin and AOV
hypothesis: If we set the free shipping threshold from the brand's margin and typical basket size instead of a number copied from a video, then the threshold pulls basket size up without eating margin because it is set to the brand's real numbers.

signal.check: The free shipping threshold is a round number copied from an example rather than calculated from the brand's margin and current AOV.

expected_effect.size: unknown, demo values seen range from about 10 to 400 in local currency, none a benchmark

risk.note: The threshold can be adjusted any time as margin or AOV changes.

prerequisites: Current AOV and gross margin per order
needs brand data: margin, AOV
steps: Pull the current average order value and gross margin per order.
Calculate a threshold slightly above current AOV that still protects margin at that basket size.
Set the free shipping rate above a flat rate at that threshold.
Decide if the threshold applies before or after coupon discounts.

test.method: Track AOV and margin per order for 8 weeks after setting the threshold.

title: Show the free shipping threshold to shoppers, do not hide it
hypothesis: If we show the free shipping threshold on the storefront through an announcement bar or cart notice, then AOV rises because a hidden threshold cannot influence a shopper's basket if they never see it.

signal.check: A free shipping threshold is configured but not visible anywhere on the storefront or in the cart.

risk.note: The bar or notice can be edited or removed any time.

prerequisites: Free shipping threshold set (SET-081)
steps: Add an announcement bar stating the free shipping threshold.
Add a cart notice showing how much more a shopper needs to spend to qualify.
Check both display correctly on mobile.

test.method: Compare AOV before and after adding the visible threshold notice.

title: Order free shipping above flat rate, and decide if it applies before or after coupons
hypothesis: If we order the free shipping method above flat rate in the zone and deliberately decide whether the minimum applies before or after coupons, then the intended margin outcome holds because the wrong order or rule can let a discounted cart get free shipping it should not.

signal.check: A WooCommerce shipping zone has free shipping and flat rate in the wrong order, or no decision has been made on coupon interaction with the threshold.

risk.note: Method order and the coupon rule can be changed any time.

prerequisites: Free shipping threshold set (SET-081)
steps: Add the Free shipping method with a minimum order amount requirement.
Drag it above Flat rate in the zone's method list.
Decide and set whether the minimum applies before or after a coupon discount.

test.method: Test a cart at the threshold with and without a coupon applied.

title: Use per-item or table rates when shipping cost scales with quantity or weight
hypothesis: If we use per-item or table rates when shipping cost scales with quantity, weight, or value, then margin holds on bulk orders because a flat per-order rate under-collects once a cart grows heavy.
does_not_apply_when: Products are small and light enough that a flat per-order rate always covers cost

signal.check: Shipping cost genuinely rises with quantity, weight, or value, but the store charges one flat per-order rate regardless of cart size.

risk.note: Bracket gaps or overlaps can leave a cart with no shipping option, so test edges after setup.

prerequisites: Real per-unit or per-weight shipping cost data
steps: Confirm real shipping cost scales meaningfully with quantity or weight for this catalog.
Set a per-item cost formula, or install a table-rate plugin for value or weight brackets.
Build brackets with no gap and no overlap between them.
Test a cart at every bracket edge.

test.method: Test carts at each bracket edge and confirm every value falls in exactly one bracket.

title: Use shipping classes for heavy items, calculated per class not per order
hypothesis: If we assign shipping classes to heavy or premium items and set calculation to per class rather than per order, then mixed carts stop undercharging because per order only charges the most expensive class once.

signal.check: Heavy or premium products have no shipping class assigned, or the zone calculates shipping per order instead of per class on a mixed cart.

risk.note: Class assignments and calculation type can be adjusted any time.

prerequisites: List of heavy or premium products needing a shipping class
steps: Create a shipping class such as Heavy under shipping settings.
Fill the per-class cost and the no-class fallback cost in the zone's flat rate method.
Set calculation type to Per class.
Assign the class to every heavy or premium product.

test.method: Test a cart with one normal item, one heavy item, and both together.

title: Keep each country in exactly one shipping zone
hypothesis: If we remove a country from the broad international zone before giving it its own market and rate, then checkout stops breaking because on Shopify a country can only live in one zone at a time.

signal.check: A country is being given its own shipping rate while it still sits inside the broader international zone.

risk.note: Zone membership can be corrected any time.

steps: Edit the international zone and uncheck the country being moved out.
Create a market for that country through Markets.
Add its own rates to the new zone.
Quote a test order to confirm only one zone now applies.

test.method: Quote a test order to that country and check it uses the new zone's rate, not the old one.

title: Set default package dimensions and weight, and assign per product where packaging differs
hypothesis: If we set a default package with dimensions and empty weight and assign a different package where packaging differs, then shipping undercharge stops compounding because volume growth multiplies any packaging gap.
