signal.check: No default package with weight and dimensions is set, or products with different packaging all share one package profile.

risk.note: Package settings can be corrected any time.

prerequisites: Real package weights and dimensions per packaging type
steps: Weigh and measure the standard shipping package.
Set it as the default package in shipping settings.
Add extra packages for any product line that ships differently.
Assign the correct package per product where it differs from the default.

test.method: Quote a shipping rate before and after setting the default package and confirm it changes.

title: Assign a fulfilment location to every zone and track inventory per location
hypothesis: If we add every warehouse as a location and assign a fulfilment location to each shipping zone, then order routing works correctly because the platform needs a location to know where inventory ships from.

signal.check: A shipping zone has no assigned fulfilment location, or inventory is not tracked per warehouse location.

risk.note: Location assignments can be corrected any time.

prerequisites: List of warehouses with addresses
steps: Add each warehouse as a location with its address.
Assign inventory per location on each product.
Assign the correct fulfilment location to each shipping zone.

test.method: Place a test order per zone and confirm it routes to the intended location.

title: Add a delivery time estimate to every shipping rate label
hypothesis: If we add a delivery time estimate to every rate label that reflects real fulfilment capability, then shipping-related tickets drop because shoppers see a promise the brand can actually keep.

signal.check: A shipping rate label reads as a bare name like Standard, with no delivery time estimate shown.

risk.note: Only promise a delivery window fulfilment can actually honor.

prerequisites: Real fulfilment and transit time data per rate
steps: Confirm the real transit time for each shipping rate with fulfilment.
Rename each rate to include the delivery estimate, for example 5 to 8 business days.
Check the estimate appears wherever shipping is mentioned, not just at checkout.

test.method: Check every live rate label shows a delivery estimate.

title: Configure local delivery or pickup only where the model needs them, and check insurance terms
hypothesis: If we configure local delivery and pickup only where the business model actually needs them and check shipping insurance terms per plan, then setup effort and cost stay matched to real need instead of unused complexity.
does_not_apply_when: The brand ships nationally or internationally only, with no local delivery or pickup model

signal.check: Local delivery or pickup is being configured without a clear local fulfilment need, or insurance terms have not been checked for the current plan.

expected_effect.size: unknown, insurance terms need a web check

risk.note: These options can be enabled or disabled any time.

steps: Confirm whether the brand's model actually needs local delivery or in-store pickup.
If so, configure the delivery radius or pickup location.
Web check the current insurance terms included in the plan versus what needs to be purchased separately.

test.method: Confirm local delivery or pickup only shows at checkout where the brand truly offers it.

title: Test carts at every rate bracket edge and every zone before launch
hypothesis: If we test carts at every bracket edge and every zone from an address in each zone before launch, then checkout failures and undercharges drop because a bracket gap or a missing rate is far cheaper to catch now than after a shopper hits it.

signal.check: Shipping rates are configured but have not been tested at bracket edges or from an address in every zone.

risk.note: This is a test pass, not a configuration change by itself.

prerequisites: Shipping zones and rates configured
steps: List every zone and its rate brackets or thresholds.
Build a test cart just below and just above each bracket edge.
Quote from at least one address in every zone.
Fix any gap, overlap, or missing rate found before launch.

test.method: Run the full bracket and zone test matrix and log any failure.

title: Vet a 3PL on reliability and speed, and sync inventory across every sales channel
hypothesis: If we vet a 3PL on integration reliability, split-shipment cost, and stock-sync speed, and sync inventory across every channel, then oversells drop because two channels can otherwise both sell the last unit.
does_not_apply_when: The brand fulfils in house on a single sales channel

signal.check: A brand is using a 3PL or selling on more than one channel with no verified inventory sync between them.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no library source for the vetting or sync rule, verify against brand data

risk.note: A 3PL can be changed, but an unsynced multichannel launch risks overselling from day one.

prerequisites: List of every sales channel selling this catalog
steps: Check the 3PL's integration reliability, split-shipment cost, and stock-sync speed with references.
Confirm every sales channel pulls from the same synced inventory count.
Run a test sale on two channels at once for a low-stock SKU to confirm sync works.
Monitor for oversells weekly in the first month.

test.method: Track oversold order count across channels for the first month.

title: Establish the brand's real tax obligations with a professional before configuring tax
hypothesis: If we establish registered locations, inventory, employees, US nexus, and EU VAT thresholds with a tax professional before configuring anything, then post-launch tax surprises drop because every source that covers tax defers to a professional and disclaims legal advice.

signal.check: Tax settings are being configured before a tax professional has confirmed the brand's actual obligations.

risk.note: Getting nexus and VAT thresholds wrong is a legal and refund cost found only after launch.

prerequisites: Access to a tax advisor for the brand's markets
steps: List registered business locations, inventory locations, and employees by country or state.
Have a tax professional confirm US nexus and EU VAT threshold status.
Only configure tax settings once these obligations are confirmed in writing.
Re-check with the advisor whenever a new market or fulfilment location is added.

test.method: Confirm a dated advisor sign-off exists before tax settings go live.

title: Set the store address before configuring tax and shipping
hypothesis: If we set the store address before configuring tax and shipping, then both settings start from the right default because they key off the store address.

signal.check: Tax or shipping setup is starting before the store address is entered in settings.

risk.note: The address can be corrected later, but tax and shipping settings built on the wrong one need re-checking.

prerequisites: Legal registered address
steps: Enter the store's legal registered address in general settings.
Confirm it is correct before opening tax or shipping settings.
Only then start tax and shipping configuration.

test.method: Check the store address is set correctly before tax or shipping configuration begins.

title: Enable the platform tax service for each registered region with its tax ID
hypothesis: If we enable the built-in tax service and add each region where tax is collected with its tax ID, then tax collects correctly because coverage matches the brand's actual registrations, not a guess.

signal.check: The built-in tax service is not enabled, or a registered region is missing its tax ID.

risk.note: Collecting tax where the brand is not registered, or missing a region where it is, is a named common error.

prerequisites: Confirmed tax obligations (SET-093)
steps: Open tax settings and confirm the base country.
Collect in a new region for each jurisdiction the brand is registered in.
Enter the tax ID for each region.
Set up duties for international markets served.

test.method: Place a test order per registered region and confirm the tax line matches intent.

title: Decide inclusive versus exclusive tax display once and keep it consistent everywhere
hypothesis: If we decide inclusive or exclusive pricing once before entering prices and display it consistently across shop, cart, and checkout, then shopper trust holds because a mismatched display makes the final price look like it changed.

signal.check: Prices display inclusive of tax on one page and exclusive on another, such as shop versus checkout.

risk.note: Inclusive is required in some markets like Japan and common in the EU, so this is a compliance decision too, not just a preference.

prerequisites: Advisor guidance on inclusive versus exclusive per market
steps: Confirm with the tax advisor whether the target market requires inclusive display.
Set the global inclusive or exclusive setting once, before entering prices.
Check shop, cart, and checkout all show the same mode.
Adjust per-market pricing under Markets if selling to both inclusive and exclusive markets.

test.method: Compare the displayed price on the shop page, cart, and checkout for the same product.

title: Build WooCommerce tax rows one per jurisdiction, to 4 decimals, with priority set
hypothesis: If we enter one tax row per jurisdiction to 4 decimals with priority set where rows overlap, then tax charges correctly because approximating many states or regions with one blanket row overcharges some and undercharges others.

signal.check: WooCommerce tax rows use one blanket rate for many states, or overlapping rows have no priority set.

expected_effect.size: unknown, rates need a web check, do not approximate

risk.note: A blanket rate or wrong priority is a common source of overcharging or undercharging tax.

prerequisites: Confirmed jurisdiction list and rates from a tax reference
steps: Set up Standard, Reduced, Zero, and any custom tax classes needed.
Assign the correct class per product.
Insert one row per jurisdiction: country, state, rate to 4 decimals, name, and priority, where a lower priority number wins.
Never approximate several states or regions with a single row.

test.method: Test one order per tax class in at least 2 jurisdictions and confirm the correct row applies.

title: Set the tax calculation basis to origin or destination, matching each state's rule
hypothesis: If we set calculate tax based on to the shop address for origin-based states and the customer shipping address for destination-based states, then tax charges correctly because using the wrong basis for a given state charges the wrong rate.

signal.check: Tax basis is set the same way for every state, with no check of which states are origin-based versus destination-based.

expected_effect.size: unknown, origin-based state list needs a web check

risk.note: Wrong basis mainly causes a wrong tax amount, not a legal filing issue, but it still needs fixing.

prerequisites: Current list of origin-based versus destination-based states
steps: Web check the current list of origin-based states for the target market.
Set the calculation basis to shop address for those states.
Set it to customer shipping address for destination-based states.
Test an order from each basis type.

test.method: Test one order to an origin-based state and one to a destination-based state.

title: Decide whether tax applies to shipping, per jurisdiction
hypothesis: If we decide the tax-on-shipping rule per jurisdiction instead of leaving a single default, then tax charges correctly because roughly half of US states tax shipping and the rest do not.

signal.check: Tax on shipping uses one default setting across every jurisdiction instead of a per-region decision.

expected_effect.size: unknown, roughly half of US states tax shipping, needs a web check

risk.note: This mainly affects tax accuracy, correctable if found.

prerequisites: Per-jurisdiction rule on taxing shipping
steps: Web check which target jurisdictions tax shipping.
Set the shipping tax class or rule per jurisdiction, not as one global default.
Turn it on for B2B sales where the advisor confirms it applies.

test.method: Test an order per jurisdiction and check the shipping tax line matches the rule.

title: Consider an automated tax service instead of manual rows for many jurisdictions
hypothesis: If we use an automated tax service instead of manual tax rows once selling into many jurisdictions, then tax upkeep drops because manual rows do not scale cleanly across dozens of regions.
does_not_apply_when: The brand sells into only 1 or 2 tax jurisdictions

signal.check: The brand sells into many tax jurisdictions and is still maintaining manual tax rows by hand.

expected_effect.size: unknown, plugin status and cost need a web check

risk.note: Switching to an automated service can be reversed, but existing manual rows need review either way.

prerequisites: Web check of the automated tax service's current status and pricing
steps: Count the number of active tax jurisdictions the brand serves.
If the count is large, web check current automated tax service pricing and requirements.
Connect the service and confirm it covers every jurisdiction the manual rows did.
Keep a human review of the transition before going live.

test.method: Compare tax line results between the manual rows and the automated service for the same test orders.

title: Test one product per tax class in at least 2 regions, and re-check after any change
hypothesis: If we test one product per tax class in at least 2 states or countries and re-open tax settings whenever a market or shipping destination changes, then a post-launch tax surprise is avoided because it is a named common error found only after launch.

signal.check: Tax settings have not been tested per class across regions, or have not been re-checked since the last new market or product was added.

risk.note: A tax surprise found after launch means refunding the difference and fixing trust.

steps: List every tax class in use.
Place a test order for each class into at least 2 different regions.
Confirm the tax line matches the intended rule for each.
Repeat this test whenever a new market, product, or shipping destination is added.

test.method: Run the tax class test matrix before launch and after every new market.
test.read_point: Pre-launch and after every new market

title: Verify every product is buyable end to end before launch
hypothesis: If we open every live product in incognito and complete add to cart through checkout, then a broken product listing is caught before a shopper hits it because a saved setting is not proof the buy flow actually works.

signal.check: Products have been configured but never test-purchased end to end from the live storefront.

risk.note: This is a test pass; failures found here are fixed before any shopper sees them.

prerequisites: Product catalog live but still password protected
steps: Open every distinct product template on the live storefront in an incognito window.
Add each to cart and reach checkout.
Confirm variant selection swaps image and price correctly.
Confirm no product shows sold out unless that is intended.

test.method: Complete a full add-to-cart and checkout-start test on every distinct product template.

title: Confirm confirmation and shipping emails actually arrive after a test order
hypothesis: If we place a real test order and confirm both the order confirmation and shipping emails actually arrive, then post-launch support tickets about missing confirmation drop because a saved notification setting does not prove delivery.

signal.check: Notification settings are configured but no test order has confirmed the emails actually land in an inbox.

risk.note: On WooCommerce especially, emails can silently fail to send without SMTP configured.

prerequisites: SMTP configured on WooCommerce
steps: Place a test order through the real checkout flow.
Confirm the confirmation email arrives in the customer inbox, not just the admin log.
Ship the test order through the real process and confirm the shipping email fires.
Repeat after any change to notification templates or SMTP settings.

test.method: Time how long it takes for both emails to arrive after a test order.
test.read_point: Pre-launch, and after any notification change

title: Run a full mobile QA pass on the live storefront before launch
hypothesis: If we run a full mobile pass on a real phone before launch, scrolling, tapping every button, and completing an add to cart and checkout start, then mobile conversion holds because desktop QA alone misses cramped navigation and unreadable text.

signal.check: The storefront has been QA tested on desktop or in a browser device emulator, but never on a real phone.

expected_effect.size: unknown, two-thirds of orders are commonly cited as mobile, unsourced, do not quote to clients

risk.note: This is a QA pass; issues found are fixed before launch.

prerequisites: A real phone, not just a browser emulator
steps: Open the live, logged-out storefront on a real phone.
Scroll every page and tap every button, including accordions and menus.
Complete an add to cart and start checkout.
Route any layout fix found to the landing page track.

test.method: Complete the mobile pass checklist and log any issue found.

title: Measure site speed before and after every app install
hypothesis: If we measure built-in speed metrics before and after every app install, then slow bloat is caught early because apps inject code and a regression is easy to trace back to the last change.

signal.check: An app was installed with no before-and-after speed check, or the app stack has grown without a recent speed review.

risk.note: An app causing a regression can be removed or its embed disabled.

prerequisites: A baseline speed measurement before any new app install
steps: Record the built-in speed metric before installing a new app.
Install and enable the app's embed.
Record the speed metric again after install.
Remove the app or its embed if speed regresses meaningfully.

test.method: Compare the speed metric immediately before and after each app install.
test.read_point: Immediately before and after every app install

title: Reconcile platform inventory against real stock counts weekly in the first month
hypothesis: If we compare platform stock to real supplier or warehouse stock weekly in the first month, then oversells are caught early because inventory drift is easiest to fix before it compounds across many orders.

signal.check: No recurring reconciliation between platform inventory counts and real stock has been scheduled since launch.

risk.note: This is a check, not a change; any drift found is corrected on discovery.

prerequisites: A source of real stock counts (supplier, 3PL, or warehouse)
steps: Pull the platform's current stock count for each top-selling SKU.
Compare against the real stock count from the supplier or warehouse.
Correct any mismatch immediately.
Repeat weekly for the first month, then move to a monthly cadence.

test.method: Log the size of the drift found at each reconciliation.
test.read_point: Weekly in month one, then monthly

title: Never quote an unsourced industry statistic in client-facing material
hypothesis: If we never repeat an unsourced industry statistic, such as a cited cart abandonment rate or conversion loss per second of delay, in client material without a current, cited source, then client trust holds because an unverifiable number found later damages credibility.

signal.check: A client-facing brief, page, or deck states an industry statistic (abandonment rate, mobile order share, conversion loss per second) with no current, checkable source.

risk.note: Removing or sourcing a claim is a quick text fix.

steps: Flag any industry statistic in a draft that has no cited, current source.
Either find a current, checkable source or remove the claim.
Prefer the brand's own data over a generic industry number wherever possible.

test.method: Review every client-facing document for an unsourced statistic before sending.
test.read_point: Before any client-facing document is sent

title: Confirm review request automation is actually sending after launch
hypothesis: If we check the reviews app's send log after launch, then the store starts building social proof on schedule because installing the app does not guarantee the automation is actually enabled and firing.

signal.check: A reviews app is installed with an automated request delay set, but no one has confirmed a request was actually sent after a real order.

risk.note: This is a verification step; a stalled automation is simple to re-enable once found.

prerequisites: Reviews app installed with automated requests configured
steps: Wait until the configured delay has passed after the first real order.
Check the reviews app's send log for that order.
If no request was sent, check the automation is enabled and the delay is set correctly.

test.method: Check the reviews app's log for the first batch of automated requests.
test.read_point: After the review request delay passes on the first real orders

title: Keep guest checkout on and never force account creation
hypothesis: If we keep guest checkout on and offer account creation only as an option during checkout, then checkout completion improves because forcing an account before buying is a named conversion mistake.
does_not_apply_when: Store runs a marketplace or membership model where formal signup is required before purchase

signal.check: Checkout requires an account before a shopper can complete a purchase.

risk.note: This setting can be toggled any time.

steps: Open checkout settings and confirm guest checkout is enabled.
Offer login or account creation as an option during checkout, not a requirement.
Confirm a shopper can complete a full purchase without ever creating an account.

test.method: Complete a test purchase as a guest with no account created.

title: Set checkout contact fields to the minimum a shopper needs to give
hypothesis: If we require only email as the contact method, phone at the shipping step, last name, and company only for B2B, then checkout friction drops because every extra required field is one more reason to abandon.

signal.check: Checkout requires fields beyond email, last name, and phone at shipping, such as a mandatory company field or a second address line for a B2C store.

risk.note: Fields can be adjusted any time.

steps: Set contact method to email, since SMS confirmation only works if a phone is given.
Set phone as required at the shipping step, not at contact.
Set last name only, not full formal fields.
Hide company and second address line unless the brand sells B2B.

test.method: Complete a test checkout and count the fields a shopper must fill.

title: Separate transactional consent from marketing consent, pre-select only where legal
hypothesis: If we use a separate marketing consent checkbox and pre-select it only where the country allows, then list growth improves without legal risk because giving an email for fulfilment is not the same as marketing consent.

signal.check: A single checkbox or no checkbox at all is being used for both fulfilment and marketing consent, or pre-selection is on in a market where it is illegal.

expected_effect.size: unknown, pre-selection can raise subscriber count but lower engagement

risk.note: Parts of Europe and the UK forbid pre-selection, so this needs a per-country web check.

prerequisites: Web check on consent pre-selection rules per target country
steps: Add a separate checkbox for email and SMS marketing consent, distinct from the order itself.
Web check whether pre-selection is legal in each target country.
Pre-select only where legal and appropriate for the brand's stage.
Leave it unchecked everywhere pre-selection is not confirmed legal.

test.method: Complete a test checkout in each target market and confirm the consent checkbox behavior matches its legal rule.

title: Brand the checkout with logo, colors, and a one-page layout within plan limits
hypothesis: If we brand the checkout with the logo, colors, and a one-page layout within the current plan's limits, then shopper trust holds through the final step because an unbranded, generic checkout can read as untrustworthy.
does_not_apply_when: Brand is on Shopify Plus and wants full custom checkout logic, which is out of scope here

signal.check: Checkout still shows the default unbranded look with no logo or brand colors applied.

risk.note: Checkout branding is a settings change, always reversible.

prerequisites: Brand logo and colors approved
steps: Open Checkout > Customize.
Add the logo and set brand colors.
Confirm a one-page checkout layout is used.
Note that full checkout logic customization is locked below the top plan tier.

test.method: View the checkout as a shopper and confirm the brand logo and colors show.

title: Use passwordless customer accounts with self-serve returns and store credit
hypothesis: If we use the newer passwordless customer accounts and enable self-serve returns and store credit, then post-purchase tickets drop because customers can act on their own account instead of emailing support.
does_not_apply_when: A marketplace model needs formal legacy signup instead

signal.check: Customer accounts still use the older password-based login, or self-serve returns and store credit are not enabled.

risk.note: This setting can be changed any time.

prerequisites: Return policy configured (SET-062)
steps: Switch customer accounts to the newer passwordless option.
Enable self-serve returns tied to the published return policy.
Enable store credit if the brand wants to offer it as a return option.

test.method: Log in as a test customer without a password and complete a self-serve return.

title: Set a per-order quantity cap when stock is scarce
hypothesis: If we set a per-order quantity cap when stock is scarce, then more customers get a chance to buy because no single order can absorb the whole limited supply.
does_not_apply_when: Stock is not scarce and there is no reason to hide inventory depth

signal.check: A limited or scarce product has no per-order quantity cap set at checkout.

expected_effect.size: demo value of 10 seen in sources

risk.note: The cap can be adjusted any time.

steps: Identify products where stock is genuinely scarce or the brand wants inventory depth hidden.
Set a per-order quantity limit at checkout for those products.
Test that a cart exceeding the limit is blocked with a clear message.

test.method: Try to add more than the cap to cart and confirm it is blocked.

title: Turn on exactly one abandoned checkout email owner, never two
hypothesis: If we let only one system, either the native platform or the ESP, own the abandoned checkout email, then shoppers stop getting duplicate or conflicting recovery emails because two owners firing at once looks unprofessional and confuses attribution.

signal.check: Both the native platform automation and an ESP flow are set to send an abandoned checkout email, or order confirmation is duplicated between native and branded emails.

risk.note: Turning one off is a quick settings change.

prerequisites: Decision on whether an ESP will own this flow
steps: Decide whether the ESP or the native platform will own the abandoned checkout email.
Turn on only that one automation.
Turn off the other so no shopper gets both.
Apply the same one-owner rule to order confirmation emails.

test.method: Abandon a test checkout and confirm only one recovery email arrives.

title: On WooCommerce, skip the cart redirect on add-to-cart and default to shop country
hypothesis: If we do not redirect to the cart on add-to-cart in a multi-product store and set default customer location to shop country rather than geolocate, then browsing continues smoothly because a redirect interrupts browsing and geolocation misreads VPN users.

signal.check: Add-to-cart redirects to the cart page in a multi-product store, or default customer location is set to Geolocate.

risk.note: Both settings can be reverted any time.

steps: Turn off redirect to cart on add-to-cart for a multi-product store.
Set default customer location to Shop country instead of Geolocate.
Test browsing several products in a row to confirm no interruption.

test.method: Add several products to cart in a row and confirm browsing is not interrupted.

title: Enable coupons with a per-user limit and a maximum spend cap
hypothesis: If we enable coupons in settings before building any discount and cap them with a per-user limit and a maximum spend where the discount is a percentage, then discount cost stays controlled because a percentage coupon with no cap can bleed margin on a large order.

signal.check: A percentage discount coupon has no maximum spend cap, or a welcome coupon has no per-user usage limit.

risk.note: An uncapped percentage coupon can be exploited on unexpectedly large carts until caught.

steps: Turn on coupon support in settings before building any discount.
Set a per-user usage limit, especially for welcome codes.
Add a maximum spend cap on any percentage-based coupon.
Use a code when attribution matters, an automatic discount otherwise.

test.method: Test a percentage coupon against a large cart and confirm the cap applies.

title: Build a separate B2B path with a price list, minimum order, and net terms
hypothesis: If we turn on the company field and build a separate price list or minimum order quantity with net terms for B2B buyers, then wholesale orders complete cleanly because a consumer checkout does not fit a business buyer's needs.
does_not_apply_when: Store sells only to individual consumers, with no business buyers

signal.check: The brand sells or wants to sell to other businesses, but checkout only offers a single consumer price list and no net terms option.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no library source for the price list, MOQ, or net terms steps, verify against brand data

risk.note: A dedicated B2B checkout path can be built alongside the existing consumer one without disrupting it.

prerequisites: Wholesale pricing and minimum order policy from the brand
steps: Turn on the company field for B2B customers.
Build a separate price list or set a minimum order quantity for wholesale buyers.
Route payment to net terms or a separate wholesale checkout.
Test a full wholesale order end to end before offering it live.

test.method: Complete a test wholesale order end to end through the new path.

title: Group target countries into markets by shared tax treatment, not geography
hypothesis: If we group countries into markets by shared tax and regulatory treatment instead of geography, then market configuration stays manageable because countries with different tax rules should not share one market setup just for being neighbors.

signal.check: Markets are being grouped by continent or region alone, with no check of shared tax and regulatory treatment.

risk.note: Market grouping can be reorganized any time.

prerequisites: Tax obligations per country confirmed
steps: List each target country's tax and regulatory treatment.
Group countries that share treatment into one market, excluding a geographic neighbor that does not share it.
Set the registered country as the default market.
Nest sub-markets where useful.

test.method: Check no market groups two countries with materially different tax rules.

title: Set a widely understood base currency and use per-market currency only with the right payment setup
hypothesis: If we pick a widely understood base currency and only offer per-market local currency once the right payments setup is active, then international checkout completion improves because checkout otherwise silently reverts to the base currency, confusing shoppers who expected local pricing.

signal.check: The store sells into multiple currency markets but checkout is not confirmed to actually charge in local currency for each.

risk.note: Currency cannot be changed after the fact without a manual reprice, so pick the base carefully up front.

prerequisites: Payments provider confirmed to support per-market currency
steps: Pick a widely understood base currency, such as USD or EUR, before entering prices.
Confirm the payments provider supports true per-market currency.
Set a rounding rule, such as ending in .95, for natural local prices.
Use a per-market catalog to exclude products or override prices where needed.

test.method: Complete a test checkout from each currency market and confirm the charge currency matches expectation.

title: Add languages with auto-translate, then a human review, and check the plan supports it
hypothesis: If we auto-translate as a baseline then have a human review it before assigning the language to its market, then international conversion improves because raw machine translation alone can misread tone or product detail.

signal.check: A target market speaks a language the storefront does not yet offer, or an added language has not had a human review since auto-translation.

expected_effect.size: unknown, free tier language limits need a web check

risk.note: Translations can be edited any time after review.

prerequisites: A reviewer fluent in the target language
steps: Web check the free tier language limit for the translation tool in use.
Add the target language and run auto-translate as a starting point.
Have a fluent human review the translation side by side with the original.
Assign the reviewed language to its matching market.

test.method: Have a native speaker review the storefront in that language before it goes live for that market.
test.read_point: Before assigning the language to a market

title: Verify the current plan actually supports per-market theme customization before promising it
hypothesis: If we verify per-market theme customization is available on the current plan before promising it to the brand, then wasted build time is avoided because this feature may need a plan above the entry tier.

signal.check: Per-market theme customization, such as swapping a hero image for one country, is being planned before confirming the current plan supports it.

expected_effect.size: unknown, plan gating needs a web check

risk.note: This is a verification step before committing build time.

prerequisites: Web check on current plan feature gating
steps: Web check whether per-market theme customization is available on the current plan.
If not available, decide whether to upgrade or skip this feature for now.
Only start the per-market theme build once availability is confirmed.

test.method: Confirm the per-market theme setting is actually accessible in admin before building on top of it.

title: Launch with a lean app stack and add one app at a time
hypothesis: If we launch with a lean stack of reviews, email, and tracking, then add one app at a time when a real need appears, then site speed and cost stay in check because apps inject code and each one slows the store.

signal.check: The launch app stack has more than the essential reviews, email, and tracking apps, or multiple apps were added at once.

expected_effect.size: unknown, 3 apps at launch is a stated rule of thumb

risk.note: Unused apps can be uninstalled any time.

steps: Launch with only reviews, email, and tracking apps, plus any free native apps genuinely needed.
Add one new app at a time only once a specific need appears.
Re-check speed after every new install.
Uninstall any app that stops earning its place.

test.method: Count active apps at launch and track speed after each new addition.
test.read_point: Launch and after every new app

title: Vet every app before install against a rating and review bar
hypothesis: If we vet every app for at least 4 stars, 100 or more reviews, recent complaint patterns, and a support response test, then post-install regrets drop because marketing claims alone do not predict reliability.

signal.check: An app is being installed based on marketing claims alone, with no check of its rating, review count, or a support response test.

expected_effect.size: unknown, 4 plus stars ideally 4.5, 100 plus reviews is a stated heuristic

risk.note: An app that fails vetting after install can still be uninstalled.

steps: Check the app's rating (4 plus, ideally 4.5 plus) and review count (100 plus, less strict for a niche need).
Scan recent reviews for a complaint pattern.
Check the developer's track record and any Built for Shopify badge.
Send a support question to the app's team and time the response before committing.

test.method: Log rating, review count, and support response time before every install.

title: Enable an app's theme embed right after installing it
hypothesis: If we enable an app's embed or blocks in the theme editor right after install, then the app actually shows to shoppers because installing it alone is not enough for it to appear.

signal.check: An app is installed but its App embed toggle in the theme editor is off.

risk.note: Embeds can be toggled any time.

steps: After installing an app, open Edit theme > App embeds.
Enable the embed or block for the newly installed app.
Confirm the app's feature actually appears on the live storefront.

test.method: Check the app's feature is visible on the live storefront right after install.

title: Pick a reviews app and request reviews from past customers before showing widgets
hypothesis: If we pick a reviews app with automated post-purchase requests and request reviews from past customers before showing widgets, then the store avoids launching at zero because an empty review widget signals a brand new, unproven store.
does_not_apply_when: This is a first-time launch with no past customers to ask

signal.check: A reviews app is being installed with no plan to request reviews from existing past customers first.

expected_effect.size: unknown, plan pricing needs a web check

risk.note: Review apps can be swapped if the chosen one underperforms.

prerequisites: List of past customers to request reviews from
steps: Choose a reviews app with automated post-purchase requests.
Before turning on the widget, send a request batch to past customers.
Turn on the widget once a baseline of real reviews exists.

test.method: Check the review count is above zero before the widget goes live.

title: Prefer native platform apps over duplicate third-party ones
hypothesis: If we prefer native apps like Search and Discovery, Bundles, Subscriptions, Inbox, and Flow where they cover the job, then app spend and speed overhead drop because a duplicate third-party app doing the same job adds cost with no extra benefit.

signal.check: A paid third-party app is doing a job a native free app already covers.

risk.note: Switching back to a third-party app is possible if the native option underperforms.

steps: List every installed app and the job it does.
Check if a native app already covers that job.
Cross-check alternatives, since this guidance favours the platform's own tools.
Switch to the native app and uninstall the duplicate if it performs as well.

test.method: Compare the native app's feature coverage against the third-party app before switching.

title: Install and activate WooCommerce plugins in the correct dependency order
hypothesis: If we install and activate the page builder and helpers first, then WooCommerce, then WooCommerce-dependent plugins, then setup errors drop because activating a dependent plugin before its parent can cause conflicts or missing features.

signal.check: WooCommerce-dependent plugins (wishlist, swatches) are being activated before WooCommerce itself, or before the page builder.

risk.note: Deactivating and reactivating in the right order fixes most conflicts.

prerequisites: Full plugin list decided for the build
steps: Install and activate the page builder and its helper plugins first.
Install and activate WooCommerce next.
Install and activate any WooCommerce-dependent plugin (wishlist, swatches) last.
Confirm no conflict or missing feature after each activation step.

test.method: Check the storefront and admin for errors after each plugin activation.

title: Configure SMTP and enable every needed transactional email event on WooCommerce
hypothesis: If we configure an SMTP plugin and enable each transactional email event the brand wants, then order emails actually send because a disabled event never fires and WooCommerce email delivery is not reliable by default.

signal.check: WooCommerce has no SMTP plugin configured, or a needed transactional email event (new order, processing, completed, refunded) is disabled.

risk.note: Silent email failure is a named common WooCommerce mistake, found only after customers complain.

prerequisites: SMTP provider account for sending
steps: Install and configure an SMTP plugin so emails actually send.
Enable each transactional email event the brand wants: new order, cancelled, failed, on hold, processing, completed, refunded, and customer emails.
Set the From name and address, and brand the emails with logo and color.
Send a test for every enabled event.

test.method: Trigger every enabled email event with a test order and confirm delivery.

title: Edit WooCommerce email templates only in a child theme
hypothesis: If we edit WooCommerce email template PHP only in a child theme, then a future parent theme update stops wiping out the customization because the child theme survives the update while a direct parent edit does not.

signal.check: Email template PHP has been edited directly in the parent theme instead of a child theme.

risk.note: Moving an existing edit to a child theme takes a one-time migration but avoids repeated loss on every theme update.

prerequisites: A child theme set up for the site
steps: Set up a child theme if one does not already exist.
Copy any email template PHP customization into the child theme's equivalent file.
Never edit email templates directly in the parent theme going forward.

test.method: Update the parent theme and confirm the email template customization survives.
test.read_point: After the next parent theme update

title: Connect Meta or TikTok sales channel apps only with owner approval
hypothesis: If we connect a Meta or TikTok sales channel app only after explicit owner approval, then account risk stays controlled because the connection needs an established business manager and page the owner controls.

signal.check: A Meta or TikTok sales channel connection is being made without a recorded owner approval.

risk.note: This connection can be removed later, but the ecomOS rule keeps Meta read only and every write an approval gate.

prerequisites: Established business manager, page, and Instagram professional account owned by the brand
steps: Confirm the brand has an established Facebook business manager, page, and Instagram professional account.
Get written owner approval before connecting the sales channel.
Log the approval and connection date in the app stack record.

test.method: Check every connected sales channel has a logged owner approval.

title: Choose subscriptions or bundles only when the product actually fits repeat purchase
hypothesis: If we choose subscriptions or bundles as a deliberate lever tied to the product, not just an app install, then adoption improves because subscriptions fit consumables that run out, not one-time or durable goods.
does_not_apply_when: Catalog is one-time or durable goods like electronics or furniture

signal.check: A subscription or bundle app is being installed without checking whether the catalog is genuinely consumable or repeat-purchase.

risk.note: The app can be removed if uptake is low.

prerequisites: Catalog reviewed for consumable or repeat-purchase fit
steps: Review the catalog for products that genuinely run out and get repurchased, such as supplements or food.
Only offer subscriptions or bundles on those products, not durable or one-time goods.
Track subscription uptake and churn once live.

test.method: Track subscription signup rate and churn on the subscription-eligible SKUs.

title: Add loyalty or rewards only when repeat purchase matters to the brand's margin
hypothesis: If we add a loyalty or rewards program only when repeat purchase genuinely matters to margin, then app spend is justified because loyalty pays off more for a repurchased catalogue than a one-time purchase brand.
does_not_apply_when: Catalog is mostly one-time or durable purchases with low repeat rate

signal.check: A loyalty app is being installed with no check of whether repeat purchase actually drives the brand's margin.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no source gives a payoff condition, verify against brand data

risk.note: The app can be removed if it does not earn its place.

prerequisites: Repeat purchase rate and its margin contribution known
steps: Check the current repeat purchase rate and how much it contributes to margin.
Only add a loyalty app if that contribution is meaningful.
Track loyalty enrollment and repeat rate change after launch.

test.method: Compare repeat purchase rate before and after the loyalty program launches.

title: Treat marketplace or multichannel listing as a deliberate decision with inventory sync
hypothesis: If we list on a marketplace or another channel only when production capacity exceeds the store's own demand and sync inventory as a launch requirement, then multichannel selling adds revenue without overselling.
does_not_apply_when: Brand has no production or stock capacity beyond its own store's current demand

signal.check: The brand is considering or already listing on a marketplace or another channel with no inventory sync plan.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no library source for the rule itself, verify against brand data

risk.note: Delisting a channel is possible, but overselling before sync is in place damages trust on every channel involved.

prerequisites: Confirmed production or stock capacity beyond current store demand
steps: Confirm the brand has spare production or stock capacity beyond its own store's demand.
Set up inventory sync between the new channel and the main store before listing.
Launch on the new channel only once sync is tested.
Monitor for oversells in the first weeks.

test.method: Track oversold orders across channels in the first month after listing.

title: Give staff custom roles and use collaborator access for agencies, not a paid seat
hypothesis: If we give staff custom roles with exact permissions and use collaborator access for developers and agencies, then account exposure drops because Orders access reveals sales figures and a shared paid seat cannot be scoped as tightly.

signal.check: Staff or an agency has a blanket admin role, or an agency holds a paid seat instead of collaborator access.

risk.note: Roles can be edited or revoked at any time.

prerequisites: Staff and agency list with intended access level
steps: List each staff member and agency with the access they actually need.
Assign custom roles instead of blanket admin.
Decide deliberately whether each role needs Orders access, since it exposes sales figures.
Use collaborator access (code plus store handle) for developers and agencies instead of a paid seat.

test.method: Audit every user's role and access level against their actual job.

title: Duplicate the theme and confirm host backups exist before every change
hypothesis: If we duplicate the theme before every change and confirm host backups exist, then a bad edit or failed launch step can be undone without the storefront going dark.

signal.check: A theme or code change is planned with no confirmed duplicate theme or host backup in place.

risk.note: This check itself carries no risk; it exists to reduce the risk of the change it precedes.

steps: Duplicate the current theme before starting any change.
Confirm the host's automatic backups are active and recent, for WooCommerce.
Use a versioned backup app if more restore depth is needed.
Route deeper hardening like login limits and malware scans to the security folder.

test.method: Confirm a working duplicate theme and a recent host backup exist before every change.
test.read_point: Before every theme or code change

title: Install and verify analytics tracking through the native integration
hypothesis: If we install tracking through the platform's native integration and verify it with a real-time view during a test session including checkout, then reporting is trustworthy from day one because a broken install found after launch loses that data forever.

signal.check: Tracking has been installed but never verified with a live real-time test session, including the checkout step.

risk.note: Data lost before tracking is verified cannot be recovered retroactively.

steps: Install analytics through the platform's native integration, not a manual code snippet.
Run a real-time test session, browsing through to the checkout step.
Confirm events show in the real-time report.
Re-verify after any theme change or app install.

test.method: Run a live real-time test session and confirm every step shows.
test.read_point: Pre-launch, and after any theme or app change

title: Read analytics over a multi-month window, not one day
hypothesis: If we read conversion and cohort reports over a multi-month window instead of a single day, then decisions get made on real trends because one day's conversion rate is not an average and a cohort needs about a year of orders to read properly.

signal.check: A conversion or performance conclusion is being drawn from a single day or a very young cohort of orders.

expected_effect.size: cohort reports need about a year of orders per source

risk.note: This is a reading discipline, not a store change.

steps: Set the reporting window to at least several weeks before drawing a conversion conclusion.
Wait roughly a year of order history before trusting a cohort report.
Route deeper funnel reading to the measurement and landing page tracks.

test.method: Check the reporting window used before any conclusion is shared with the founder.

title: Follow the dependency-ordered launch sequence, step by step
hypothesis: If we follow the setup order of identity, payments, tax, shipping and package weights, domain and email, tracking and legal pages, test order, then password removal, then rework drops because later steps depend on earlier ones being correct.

signal.check: Setup steps are being done out of dependency order, such as tax before identity or a test order before shipping is configured.

risk.note: Reordering work does not change any setting by itself.

steps: Complete legal identity, then payments, then tax.
Complete shipping and package weights next.
Complete domain, business email, tracking, and legal pages.
Run the test order only after all of the above.
Remove the password only after the test order passes.

test.method: Check the launch checklist for any step completed out of this order.

title: Close every setup step with the action a real customer would take
hypothesis: If we close every setup step with a real customer action, such as a test order, a rate quote, a footer link click, or an incognito visit, then hidden breakage is caught because a saved setting is not proof it actually works.

signal.check: A setup step is being marked done because the setting was saved, with no matching customer-style action taken to confirm it works.

risk.note: This is a verification habit, not a store change.

steps: For every setup step, define the matching customer action that proves it works.
Perform that action: a test order, a rate quote, a link click, or an incognito visit.
Only mark the step done once the action succeeds, not when the setting is saved.

test.method: Spot check 5 completed setup steps and confirm each has a matching passed customer action.

title: Run real test orders through the real gateway and fulfilment before launch
hypothesis: If we run test mode orders then real orders through the real gateway and real fulfilment, including one address per zone and one product per tax class, then launch day failures drop because a simulated test order is not proof the real pipeline works end to end.

signal.check: Only a simulated or sandbox test order has been run, with no real order through the real gateway and fulfilment pipeline.

risk.note: This test costs a small real transaction but catches issues a simulated order cannot.

prerequisites: Payment gateway live
Warehouse or fulfilment integration connected
steps: Run test mode orders first at one address per zone and one product per tax class.
Switch to live and place one small real order through the real gateway.
Confirm it reaches fulfilment and, if a warehouse app is connected, that tracking flows back.
Test on a real phone as well as desktop.
Confirm the confirmation email arrives.

test.method: Complete a real order through the full pipeline and confirm every step (payment, tax, shipping, email, fulfilment) works.

title: Verify the live, logged-out storefront in incognito, clicking every interactive element
hypothesis: If we verify the live, logged-out storefront in an incognito window and click every interactive element, then broken elements are caught before shoppers hit them because AI-built accordions and similar elements can render but fail to open.

signal.check: The storefront has only been checked in the theme editor preview, not on the live, logged-out URL in incognito.

risk.note: This is a QA pass; issues found are fixed before launch.

steps: Open the storefront's live URL in an incognito window, logged out.
Click every accordion, tab, menu item, and interactive element.
Confirm each one actually opens or resolves, not just renders.

test.method: Complete the full click-through pass and log anything that renders but does not respond.

title: Remove the password only after the checklist passes, then browse as a first-time visitor
hypothesis: If we remove the password only after the pre-launch checklist passes and then browse the domain as a first-time visitor, then launch quality holds because a store made public before the checklist passes exposes real gaps to real shoppers.

signal.check: Removing the password or switching to Live is being planned before the pre-launch checklist has fully passed.

risk.note: The password can be re-enabled quickly if a serious issue is found right after launch.

prerequisites: Pre-launch checklist fully passed
steps: Confirm every row of the pre-launch checklist has passed.
Remove the password or switch WooCommerce site visibility to Live.
Confirm the intended theme shows as live.
Browse the domain in a new incognito tab as a first-time visitor: homepage, product, add to cart, checkout start.

test.method: Complete the first-time-visitor browse right after going live and confirm nothing is broken.

title: Launch imperfect once the checklist passes, then collect feedback
hypothesis: If we launch once the checklist passes rather than waiting for a perfect storefront, then real feedback starts flowing sooner because real shopper behavior teaches more than more pre-launch polishing.

signal.check: Launch is being delayed for polish beyond the pre-launch checklist, with no specific blocking issue remaining.

risk.note: Post-launch issues found from real feedback can still be fixed quickly.

prerequisites: Pre-launch checklist fully passed
steps: Confirm the pre-launch checklist has fully passed.
Launch even if some non-blocking polish items remain.
Set up a plan to collect and act on real shopper feedback in the first weeks.

test.method: Track time from checklist pass to actual launch date.

title: Give the AI build agent real inputs before it starts building
hypothesis: If we give the AI agent the real products, collections, and an inspiration folder with logo, photos, and screenshots before it builds, then output quality improves because the agent designs around what actually exists, not a placeholder guess.

signal.check: An AI build session is starting with no real products, collections, or brand asset folder in place yet.

risk.note: This is a preparation step before any build session.

prerequisites: Products and collections already in the store
Inspiration folder with logo, photos, and screenshots
steps: Confirm real products and collections already exist in the store.
Assemble an inspiration folder with logo versions, product photos, and screenshots.
Include any spec or framework document the brand already has.
Remind the agent of the real product count during the build, not just at the start.

test.method: Check the agent's output references real products and assets, not placeholders.

title: Let the AI agent interview you and propose a plan before it builds anything
hypothesis: If we let the agent read the theme and interview us on direction, sections, fonts, and preview method before writing anything, then rework drops because the plan is agreed before code is written, not after.

signal.check: An AI build session jumps straight to writing sections without first reading the theme and confirming a plan.

risk.note: This only shapes the plan before build; nothing is written to the store yet.

prerequisites: AI agent has read access to the current theme
steps: Ask the agent to read the current theme first.
Have it ask about direction, required sections, fonts, and preview method.
Review and confirm its proposed plan before it writes any section.

test.method: Confirm a written plan exists and was approved before any section was built.
test.read_point: Before the first section is built

title: Ask for one storefront change per AI prompt and verify it live before the next
hypothesis: If we ask for one storefront change per prompt and verify it live before issuing the next, then broken PDP elements never reach shoppers because a bundled request that lands 3 of 4 changes can leave the missing piece silently broken.

signal.check: An AI prompt is requesting several distinct storefront changes at once, with no plan to verify each before the next.

expected_effect.size: one documented case landed 3 of 4 bundled changes

risk.note: A missed change in a bundled request can go unnoticed until a shopper hits it.

steps: Break a multi-part request into single, discrete changes.
Ask for one change per prompt.
Verify that change live in the preview before issuing the next prompt.
Re-issue any missing piece alone if a bundled request was already sent.

test.method: Verify each requested change live before moving to the next prompt.

title: Preview AI theme work privately, never on the public storefront URL
hypothesis: If we preview AI theme work on a local dev server or an unpublished theme with the store password, then unfinished work never reaches shoppers because the preview password is the store password, not the account password.

signal.check: AI-built changes are being reviewed on a URL a shopper could reach, rather than a local dev server or password-gated unpublished theme.

risk.note: This is a review-process discipline, not a store setting.

steps: Preview on a local dev server or an unpublished duplicate theme.
Enter the storefront password from Online Store > Preferences, not the account password.
Never share the live public URL as the review link for unfinished work.

test.method: Confirm the review link used is the local dev or unpublished preview, not the public domain.

title: Pull and push theme code through the CLI on a duplicated theme only
hypothesis: If we pull and push theme code through the CLI on a duplicated theme only, with a human running the login and reading every permission prompt, then the live theme stays safe because pulling or pushing the live theme directly removes the restore point.

signal.check: A CLI pull or push is targeting the live theme directly, or the login step was not run and confirmed by a human.

risk.note: A push straight to the live theme with no duplicate has no restore point if it fails.

prerequisites: Node.js, Git, and the Shopify CLI installed
Theme already duplicated in admin
steps: Duplicate the live theme in admin, or confirm the agent duplicated it.
Have a human run the CLI login command and pick the correct account.
Pull the duplicate theme by name or ID, never the live theme.
Push changes unpublished, review in the theme editor, then publish only with owner approval.

test.method: Confirm the theme list shows the duplicate and the untouched live theme before and after the CLI session.
test.read_point: Before and after every CLI session

title: Add custom Liquid sections correctly: assign the product template and select the product
hypothesis: If we assign the product template and select the product in the section settings after adding a custom Liquid section, then it actually renders because a custom section with no product selected shows empty.

signal.check: A custom Liquid section has been added via Edit Code but shows empty because no product is selected in its settings.

risk.note: An empty custom section reaching a shopper looks broken until fixed.

prerequisites: Custom section file added to the duplicate theme
steps: Add the section file under Edit code > Sections on the duplicate theme.
Create a product template that hides the default sections and adds the custom one.
In the section's settings, select the specific product it should render for.
Assign the template to that product.
To update the section later, paste over the same file, never create a second one.

test.method: View the product on the live theme and confirm the custom section renders with content, not empty.

title: Treat AI theme output as a draft that needs a manual QA pass
hypothesis: If we prune duplicate sections, resize icons, click every interactive element, and check for oversized images after any AI theme build, then launch quality holds because AI output is a draft, not a finished storefront.

signal.check: AI-generated theme sections are being prepared for launch without a manual pass for duplicate sections, icon sizing, interactivity, and image weight.

risk.note: This is a QA pass on already-built sections.

prerequisites: AI-generated sections built on a duplicate theme
steps: Scan for and remove duplicate sections the AI may have created.
Resize any oversized icon.
Click every interactive element to confirm it works.
Check no image is oversized in file weight.
Run a mobile pass, since AI build sources skip this step.

test.method: Complete the manual QA checklist on every AI-built section before publishing.
test.read_point: Before publishing any AI-built theme section

title: Clone a competitor's layout pattern only, never their text, logo, product, or faces
hypothesis: If we clone a competitor's layout or interaction pattern only, never its text, logo, products, or faces, then the store stays original and out of legal trouble because copying identifiable content, not just structure, crosses a real line.

signal.check: A design reference from a competitor is being used for more than layout and mood, such as reused text, logo, product photos, or model faces.

risk.note: Copied text, logos, products, or faces are a legal and trust risk if published.

steps: Use a competitor reference only for layout and interaction pattern, never wording or imagery.
Write original copy and use the brand's own product photos.
Refuse any request to swap a logo onto a cloned competitor page.

test.method: Compare the final page against the competitor reference for any copied text, logo, product, or face.

title: Differentiate copy and imagery whenever one template is reused across products
hypothesis: If we reuse one product template's structure across many SKUs but write distinct copy and imagery for each, then the store keeps a unique feel because reusing structure and content together reads as generic.

signal.check: The same product template is being reused across many SKUs with the same copy and imagery pattern, only the product swapped.

risk.note: Copy and imagery can be revised any time without touching the template structure.

prerequisites: A working product template structure
steps: Reuse the template structure and metafields for what genuinely is common across products.
Write distinct copy for each product's short and long description.
Use distinct product photography for each SKU, not a shared stock look.
Never reuse a competitor's page structure with only the logo swapped.

test.method: Spot check 5 product pages built from the same template for repeated copy or imagery.

title: Configure the order fulfilment flow correctly for physical and backordered items
hypothesis: If we keep auto-fulfil off for physical goods, move orders to Completed only after shipping, and split multi-item orders when one item is backordered, then fulfilment accuracy improves because a physical order marked fulfilled before it ships misleads the customer.

signal.check: Auto-fulfil is on for physical goods, or a multi-item order with one backordered item is not being split so the in-stock items can ship now.

risk.note: Order flow settings can be adjusted any time.

steps: Turn off auto-fulfil for physical goods, keeping it on only for gift cards.
On WooCommerce, move an order from Processing to Completed only after it actually ships.
On Shopify, let the tracking number trigger the shipping confirmation email.
Split a multi-item order and ship the in-stock items now when one item is backordered.

test.method: Check a sample of recent orders for correct status timing against real ship dates.

title: Edit notification templates sparingly and send a test after every change
hypothesis: If we edit fixed notification templates sparingly and send a test after any edit, then customers keep getting reliable order emails because an untested edit can silently break the template.

signal.check: A notification template was edited with no test send to confirm it still renders and delivers correctly.

risk.note: A broken notification template can go unnoticed until a customer reports a missing or garbled email.

steps: Make the minimum edit needed to a notification template.
Send a test of that specific notification.
Confirm it renders correctly and arrives before considering the edit done.

test.method: Send a test notification after every template edit.

title: Classify support tickets weekly to find thin product pages or policies
hypothesis: If we classify support tickets weekly in the first weeks after launch, then the real fix gets made because product questions point to a thin product page and shipping questions point to a thin shipping policy, not a notification email problem.

signal.check: Support tickets are being answered one by one with no weekly classification to spot a repeated root cause.

risk.note: This is a review habit, not a store change by itself.

steps: Tag each incoming ticket by topic: product question, shipping question, order status, or other.
Review the tag counts weekly for the first month.
If product questions dominate, fix the product page, not the notification emails.
If shipping questions dominate, fix the shipping policy, not the notification emails.

test.method: Track ticket topic mix week over week and confirm the dominant category gets a page or policy fix, not an email edit.

title: Re-run shipping and tax checks whenever a product, zone, market, app, or theme changes
hypothesis: If we re-run the shipping and tax checks whenever a product, zone, market, app, or theme changes, then post-launch tax and shipping surprises drop because a change that looks unrelated can quietly shift a rate or a tax rule.

signal.check: A product, zone, market, app, or theme change has happened since launch with no shipping or tax re-check afterward.

risk.note: Skipping this re-check is how a tax or shipping surprise slips out after launch.

prerequisites: Shipping and tax checklists (5.3) from the original launch
steps: Note any change to products, zones, markets, apps, or theme after launch.
Re-run the shipping rate quote test for the affected zones.
Re-run the tax test for the affected jurisdictions.
Fix anything that shifted before the change goes fully live.

test.method: Re-run the shipping and tax checklist after each qualifying change.
test.read_point: After every product, zone, market, app, or theme change

title: Consolidate apps that do the same job instead of running duplicates
hypothesis: If we consolidate to one reviews app, one abandoned checkout flow, and one search app instead of running duplicates, then speed and cost improve because two apps doing the same job add weight and spend with no extra benefit.

signal.check: More than one app is doing the same job, such as two review apps or two abandoned checkout flows running at once.

risk.note: Uninstalling the duplicate can be reversed if the remaining app underperforms.

prerequisites: Full current app list with each app's job noted
steps: List every installed app and the specific job it does.
Flag any job covered by more than one app.
Keep the better performing one and uninstall the duplicate.
Disable its embed and confirm the remaining app still covers the job.

test.method: Confirm each core job (reviews, abandoned checkout, search) has exactly one active app after the audit.

title: Time-bound agency collaborator access and revoke it when the engagement ends
hypothesis: If we grant agency collaborator access as time-bound and revoke it when the engagement ends, then account exposure drops because a former agency holding live access is a needless standing risk.

signal.check: An agency or contractor still holds collaborator or staff access after their engagement has ended.

risk.note: Revoking access can be undone by re-issuing a new code if the agency returns.

prerequisites: List of active agency and contractor engagements with end dates
steps: Note the expected end date when granting any agency collaborator access.
Set a reminder to review access at that date.
Revoke the collaborator code once the engagement ends, and re-issue fresh if it resumes.

test.method: Audit collaborator access quarterly against the current list of active engagements.
test.read_point: Quarterly, and at every engagement end

title: Register matching domain TLDs beyond .com to block squatters
hypothesis: If we register the store's brand name across a few extra common domain extensions when we buy the primary domain, then brand impersonation risk drops because a lookalike site cannot use an obvious near match of the real domain.

signal.check: The brand name's main domain is registered but common alternate extensions for the same name are still open to anyone.

risk.note: Extra domains cost only renewal fees and can be dropped later if unused.

prerequisites: Primary domain already chosen and available
steps: Check availability of the brand name on 2 to 3 extra common extensions.
Register any that are available and affordable.
Redirect each extra domain to the primary site.
Renew alongside the primary domain each year.

test.method: Check yearly whether a lookalike domain using an open extension has appeared.
test.read_point: Once a year at domain renewal

title: Publish every page before linking it in a menu or footer
hypothesis: If we publish every policy or info page before linking it in a menu, then broken links drop because an unpublished page has no resolvable URL to link to.

signal.check: A menu or footer item points at a page that is still a draft, not published.

risk.note: Publishing a page early with placeholder text is easy to fix by editing it further.

prerequisites: Page content drafted
steps: Write and save the page.
Publish the page, not just save it as a draft.
Add the published page to the menu or footer.
Click the live link to confirm it resolves.

test.method: Click every footer and menu link on the live site.
test.read_point: Before launch and after adding any new page

title: Add social links to store settings before launch
hypothesis: If we add the brand's social links, starting with the platform it is most active on, to store settings before launch, then first-time visitor trust improves because many shoppers check social proof before buying and a missing link reads as a less credible store.

signal.check: The store has active social accounts but no links to them anywhere on the site.

risk.note: Links can be added or removed at any time with no side effects.

prerequisites: At least one active social account
steps: List every active social account for the brand.
Add each profile link in the store's brand or social settings.
Confirm the icons or links appear in the header or footer.
Click each link to confirm it opens the right profile.

test.method: Compare trust related support questions or bounce rate before and after adding links.

title: Use theme or section level custom CSS instead of editing core files
hypothesis: If we make small design tweaks with theme level or section level custom CSS instead of editing core theme files, then the risk of breaking the theme drops because the override sits in one safe layer that is easy to find and remove.

signal.check: A small visual tweak is about to be made by editing a core theme file directly.

risk.note: A CSS override can be deleted without touching the underlying theme code.

steps: Identify the specific visual change needed.
Open the theme's custom CSS field at the theme or section level.
Write the smallest CSS rule that achieves the change.
Preview and confirm nothing else on the page shifted.

test.method: Compare the page before and after the CSS change on desktop and mobile.

title: Build the homepage in a fixed, conversion focused section order
hypothesis: If we build the homepage in a fixed order, hero then a trust or USP row then bestsellers then collections then about then testimonials, then new visitors reach proof and product faster because the layout follows a tested pattern instead of an arbitrary one.

signal.check: The homepage has no bestseller or trust section, or key sections sit far below the fold.

risk.note: Sections can be reordered again with no data loss.

prerequisites: Hero image, at least one bestseller collection, and testimonials ready
steps: List the sections available for the homepage.
Order them hero, USP or trust row, bestsellers, collection list, about, testimonials.
Remove any leftover default sections not in this order.
Preview on mobile and desktop and adjust spacing.

test.method: Compare scroll depth and clicks to product pages before and after reordering.

title: Set a focal point on hero and banner images before publishing
hypothesis: If we set a focal point on hero and banner images before publishing, then the key subject stays visible on every device because automatic cropping keeps that point in frame instead of cutting it off on mobile.

signal.check: A hero or banner image crops out the product or model on mobile preview.

risk.note: The focal point can be adjusted again at any time.

prerequisites: Hero image uploaded
steps: Open the image editor on the hero or banner image.
Set the focal point to the key subject, such as a face or product.
Preview the crop on mobile, tablet and desktop.
Adjust the focal point if any view still cuts off the subject.

test.method: Review the hero image on 3 common screen widths after publishing.

title: Reserve a new page template for real layout differences only
hypothesis: If we keep one shared default template per page type and only branch to a separate template when a record's layout truly differs, using a metafield when only the content differs, then build and upkeep time drops because most records never need a custom template at all.

signal.check: A new collection or product got its own full template just to show different text or an image, not a different layout.

risk.note: Consolidating templates back to metafields is reversible page by page.

prerequisites: Default template exists
steps: List every custom template currently in use.
For each one, check if only content differs from the default.
Move content only differences to a metafield on the default template.
Delete the now unneeded custom template.

test.method: Count custom templates before and after the cleanup.

title: Run a time boxed promotion in the announcement bar with a countdown
hypothesis: If we run a time boxed promotion in the announcement bar with a visible countdown timer, then clicks to the promoted collection improve because a visible deadline adds urgency that plain text does not.

signal.check: A live promotion is announced in the bar with no end date or countdown shown.

risk.note: The countdown and message can be removed as soon as the promotion ends.

prerequisites: An active, time boxed promotion
steps: Set the promotion's real end date and time.
Add the countdown timer block to the announcement bar.
Link the bar to the promoted collection or discount.
Remove the bar once the promotion ends.

test.method: Compare click through rate on the bar with and without a countdown, on similar promotions.

title: Add a header country or region selector for multi market stores
hypothesis: If we add a country or region selector to the header for a store selling into more than one market, then checkout drop off from wrong pricing or stock drops because shoppers can confirm they are seeing the right region before they browse.
does_not_apply_when: Store sells into only one country or region

signal.check: The store sells into more than one market but shows only one default region with no way to switch.

risk.note: Low risk change that can be reverted if it does not help.

prerequisites: More than one market or region configured
steps: Enable the country or region selector in header settings.
Confirm it lists every configured market.
Test that switching region updates price, currency and stock correctly.
Place the selector somewhere visible, not buried in a menu.

test.method: Compare checkout completion by region before and after adding the selector.
test.read_point: A few weeks after enabling it

title: Turn on a sticky header so navigation and cart stay reachable
hypothesis: If we turn on a sticky header so navigation and cart stay visible while a shopper scrolls, then return to menu friction drops because shoppers do not have to scroll back to the top to search, browse categories or open the cart.

signal.check: The header disappears on scroll and shoppers must scroll up to reach navigation or the cart.

risk.note: Sticky header can be turned off again if it causes layout problems on mobile.

steps: Enable the sticky header option in theme settings.
Check it does not overlap content on mobile.
Confirm the cart icon and search stay reachable while scrolling.
Test on the longest page in the catalog.

test.method: Compare cart and search usage before and after enabling sticky header.

title: Test a cart drawer against a full cart page before assuming one wins
hypothesis: If we test a cart drawer against a full cart page instead of assuming one converts better, then the store keeps the format that actually performs for its own shoppers because the better choice varies by catalog and audience.

signal.check: The store picked cart drawer or cart page by preference alone, with no comparison run.

risk.note: Low risk change that can be reverted if it does not help.

prerequisites: Enough traffic to run a comparison
steps: Pick a test window and traffic split method.
Run the cart drawer for one segment and the cart page for another, or alternate by period.
Track add to cart through checkout start for each.
Keep the format with the higher cart to checkout rate.

test.method: Split test or sequential test comparing cart drawer against cart page.

title: Add a free shipping progress bar that updates live in the cart
